Local Law and Eigenvector Delocalization for Random Lifts

Jiaoyang Huang†\dagger  Ruizhe Xu‡\ddagger
Abstract

We establish a quantitative local law for random NN-lifts of a fixed finite connected simple graph with minimum degree at least three. Away from the singular energies of the universal-cover spectrum, we obtain high-probability entrywise Green’s function estimates down to spectral scales (log⁡N)C/N(\log N)^{C}/N, uniformly in the bulk and near regular edges and cusps. As a consequence, we establish complete eigenvector delocalization: every normalized eigenvector uu whose eigenvalue stays a small but fixed positive distance away from the singular energies satisfies ‖u‖∞⩽(log⁡N)C/N\|u\|_{\infty}\leqslant(\log N)^{C}/\sqrt{N} with high probability.

22footnotetext: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, New York University. Email: jh4427@nyu.edu.33footnotetext: Department of Mathematics, The University of Hong Kong. Email: ruizhexu.math@gmail.com.

1 Introduction and main results

1.1 Motivation

Let ℋ{\mathcal{H}} be a fixed finite connected simple base graph. An NN-lift of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is a graph 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} obtained by replacing each vertex of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} with a fiber of NN vertices and, for each edge of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, joining the corresponding fibers by perfect matching. We denote by 𝖦N​(ℋ){\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}) the collection of all such NN-lifts. A random NN-lift 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is obtained by sampling an element uniformly at random from 𝖦N​(ℋ){\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}). The local limit of random NN-lifts of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is described by the universal covering tree 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. More precisely, 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} is a tree equipped with a covering map π:𝒳→ℋ\pi:{\mathcal{X}}\to{\mathcal{H}} that induces a bijection between the neighbors of each vertex xx in 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} and those of π⁡(x)\pi(x). Intuitively, 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} is obtained by unfolding the cycles of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, preserving its local adjacency structure while eliminating cycles. The covering map π\pi also assigns each vertex xx in 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} a type π⁡(x)\pi(x) in ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, which determines its degree and the types of its neighbors. In particular, random lifts of a dd-regular base graph are themselves dd-regular graphs with the homogeneous dd-regular tree as their universal cover, whereas a general base graph may give rise to a nonregular universal cover with several geometrically distinct local types.

The study of random lifts is motivated by several complementary perspectives, ranging from sparse random matrix theory and quantum ergodicity to spectral geometry and theoretical computer science. As sparse random matrix models, random lifts have prescribed, potentially nonhomogeneous local geometry, complementing the extensively studied Erdős–Rényi and random regular graph models; For further discussion, see Related works below and [37]. They also have a natural connection with quantum ergodicity, which studies the spatial distribution of eigenfunctions on large finite systems whose local geometry approaches an infinite limiting space. For random NN-lifts of a fixed base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, this limiting geometry is precisely the universal cover 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. Random lifts therefore provide a natural discrete model for investigating how the geometry of the universal cover governs not only the spectrum, but also the spatial behavior of eigenfunctions on large random coverings [6, 8, 10, 11]. From the perspective of spectral geometry, random lifts may be viewed as discrete analogues of random finite-sheeted coverings of a fixed hyperbolic surface. In both settings, one constructs increasingly large random coverings of a fixed base object while preserving its universal cover, which is a tree in the graph setting and the hyperbolic plane in the surface setting. This parallel leads naturally to related spectral questions, including the behavior of new eigenvalues, spectral gaps, and the influence of the universal cover on the spectrum of large finite coverings [49, 50]. Finally, random lifts also play an important role in theoretical computer science and coding theory, providing a probabilistic way to construct large sparse graphs from prescribed finite templates, with well-studied connectivity and expansion properties [4, 5].

A central question concerns the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of random lifts. The spectrum of a lift naturally separates into two parts. Functions that are constant on each fiber form an invariant subspace on which the adjacency operator is identified with that of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. Its eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, are the old eigenvalues. The eigenvalues on the orthogonal complement are the new eigenvalues. Since the base graph is fixed, the old spectrum has bounded dimension, whereas the new eigenvalues account for almost all of the spectrum as N→∞N\to\infty. The principal spectral questions therefore concern the location and local distribution of these new eigenvalues.

The question of spectral location is closely related to the Ramanujan property, classically studied in the special case of dd-regular graphs. A dd-regular graph is Ramanujan if all eigenvalues other than the trivial eigenvalues ±d\pm d lie in [−2​d−1,2​d−1][-2\sqrt{d-1},2\sqrt{d-1}], the spectrum of the infinite dd-regular tree [48]. Friedman’s proof of Alon’s conjecture shows that random dd-regular graphs are asymptotically Ramanujan, and Bordenave subsequently gave another proof and an extension to random lifts [31, 18]. More recently, Huang, McKenzie, and Yau proved edge universality for every fixed d⩾3d\geqslant 3: after centering and an appropriate degree-dependent N2/3N^{2/3} rescaling, the extreme nontrivial eigenvalues have Tracy–Widom1 limits. The joint behavior of the two spectral edges implies that asymptotically about 69%69\% of random dd-regular graphs are Ramanujan [40].

For lifts of a general base graph, the corresponding relative question asks whether all new eigenvalues lie in [−ρ,ρ][-\rho,\rho], where ρ\rho is the spectral radius of the universal cover. Early bounds and approaches to this problem were developed by Friedman, Linial and Puder, Lubetzky, Sudakov, and Vu, and Puder [30, 46, 47, 51]. A major breakthrough was achieved by Bordenave and Collins, who proved that, for general fixed base graphs, the new spectrum converges in probability, in Hausdorff distance, to the spectrum of the universal cover [19]. This also rules out new eigenvalues at a fixed positive distance inside gaps of the limiting spectrum, not merely outside [−ρ,ρ][-\rho,\rho]. More recently, a new approach to strong convergence of random matrices based on the polynomial method has been developed in [25, 26] by Chen, Garza-Vargas, Tropp, and van Handel, yielding quantitative bounds on the convergence of extreme eigenvalues.

An equally fundamental question concerns eigenvector delocalization: to what extent can the mass of an eigenvector concentrate on a small part of the graph? For locally tree-like regular graphs, non-concentration estimates were established by Brooks and Lindenstrauss [24], while quantum ergodicity results provide averaged forms of spatial delocalization, including for random lifts under suitable assumptions [8, 6, 10, 11]. Stronger results have been obtained for fixed-degree random regular graphs, where complete eigenvector delocalization provides uniform bounds on the coordinates of all normalized eigenvectors [15, 42]. These developments naturally motivate the question of whether similarly strong delocalization bounds hold for random lifts with a prescribed nonhomogeneous local structure.

A local law provides a common framework for studying the local eigenvalue density and eigenvector delocalization. Its basic object is the Green’s function G⁡(z):=(A−z)−1G(z):=(A-z)^{-1} with z=E+i​η∈ℂ+,z=E+\mathrm{i}\eta\in\mathbb{C}_{+}, where AA denotes the adjacency matrix of the graph. The parameter η\eta determines the spectral resolution of the Green’s function: as η\eta decreases, G⁡(z)G(z) probes increasingly fine spectral scales. This allows Green’s function estimates to provide information about both eigenvalues and eigenvectors. In the special case of random dd-regular graphs, local laws were first established in growing-degree regimes [16] and subsequently in the fixed-degree setting [15, 42]. These results naturally motivate the extension of local laws to random lifts with potentially nonhomogeneous universal covers.

The purpose of the present paper is to establish a local law and to prove complete eigenvector delocalization for random lifts throughout the regular spectral regime. Under the assumptions stated below, we obtain quantitative Green’s function estimates down to spectral scales of order (log⁡N)C/N(\log N)^{C}/N, for a sufficiently large constant CC, uniformly in the stable bulk and in neighborhoods of all regular edges and regular cusps. Thus, apart from the singular energies of the universal-cover spectrum, our local law covers the full regular spectrum. As consequences, it identifies the local eigenvalue density with that of the universal cover in the bulk and implies complete delocalization of all eigenvectors whose eigenvalues stay away from the singular energies. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first local law and complete eigenvector delocalization results covering the bulk, regular edges, and regular cusps for random lifts of general fixed base graphs.

Related works.

Strong convergence provides a global spectral approach to random lifts, whose adjacency matrices can be represented as matrix-valued polynomials in random permutation matrices. Strong convergence and quantitative norm estimates for such polynomials were established and further developed in [19, 20]. More recent approaches based on polynomial and rational trace expansions yield quantitative strong convergence [25, 26]. Related spectral bounds have been obtained through non-backtracking methods [17] and matrix concentration and free-probability techniques [13, 23]. These results provide global spectral control, but do not directly yield Green’s function estimates on nearly microscopic scales.

For random regular graphs, bulk universality was first established in growing-degree regimes [14], and has recently been proved for every fixed degree d⩾3d\geqslant 3 [33]. Beyond eigenvalue statistics, the eigenvector moment flow [22] has yielded Gaussian eigenvector statistics for sparse random graphs in growing-degree regimes [21]. In the fixed-degree setting, Gaussian-wave limits have been established for almost eigenvectors and edge eigenvectors [12, 34]. Related questions of quantum ergodicity and delocalization are discussed in [7, 9].

For Erdős–Rényi graphs, local laws and complete eigenvector delocalization have been established in various sparsity regimes, extending to logarithmic expected degrees [28, 36, 2]. Bulk and edge universality were developed in [27, 38]. At greater sparsity, edge statistics require deterministic and random corrections [45, 39, 35, 43], while degree fluctuations can produce localized or semilocalized edge eigenvectors [1, 3]. Gaussian statistics of extremal eigenvectors have also been established for sparse random matrices [32].

1.2 Main results: Local law and Delocalization

To state our main results, we first introduce the spectral structure of the universal cover of the base graph, which describes the limiting spectral behavior of random lifts. A detailed account of the relevant results is given in Section 2.1; here we briefly summarize only those facts needed for the formulation of our main theorems.

Let 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} be the universal cover of the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. Its density-of-states measure is encoded by the diagonal Green functions of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}. More precisely, for each vertex type i∈ℍi\in{\mathbb{H}}, let mi​(z)m_{i}(z) denote the diagonal Green function at a vertex of type ii, and set

mℋ​(z):=1|ℍ|​∑i∈ℍmi​(z).m_{{\mathcal{H}}}(z):=\frac{1}{|{\mathbb{H}}|}\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{H}}}m_{i}(z).

By the spectral theorem, there is a probability measure νℋ\nu_{{\mathcal{H}}} on ℝ\mathbb{R} such that

mℋ​(z)=∫ℝ1τ−z​νℋ​(𝑑τ).m_{{\mathcal{H}}}(z)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{1}{\tau-z}\,\nu_{{\mathcal{H}}}(\mathrm{d}\tau).

The measure νℋ\nu_{{\mathcal{H}}} consists of an absolutely continuous part, with density denoted by ρℋ\rho_{{\mathcal{H}}}, together with possibly finitely many atoms. Thus, schematically,

νℋ​(d​τ)=ρℋ​(τ)​d​τ+∑τjwτj​δτj​(d​τ),\nu_{{\mathcal{H}}}(\mathrm{d}\tau)=\rho_{{\mathcal{H}}}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau+\sum_{\tau_{j}}w_{\tau_{j}}\,\delta_{\tau_{j}}(\mathrm{d}\tau), (1.1)

where {τj}\{\tau_{j}\} is the finite set of atomic energies and wτj>0w_{\tau_{j}}>0 denotes the corresponding atomic weight. See Lemma 2.2 and Remark 2.3 for details.

The spectral measure of a general universal cover need not be regular at every energy. Besides the atoms, there may be exceptional energies at which the absolutely continuous density becomes singular, for instance by diverging as the energy approaches the exceptional point. We refer to these exceptional points collectively as the singular energies and exclude them from the spectral regimes considered below. Away from the singular energies, the absolutely continuous spectrum decomposes into the standard regular regimes: regular bulk, where ρℋ\rho_{{\mathcal{H}}} is positive and regular; regular edges, which mark the endpoints of spectral bands; and regular cusps, where the endpoints of two neighboring spectral bands meet as the gap between them closes. See Figure 1 and Definition 2.5 for details.

To compare the Green’s function of a finite lift with that of the universal cover, we need the local geometry of the lift to remain tree-like. We therefore introduce the following deterministic class Ω¯\bar{\Omega} of lifts with this typical local geometry. In Proposition 2.1 below, we show that a uniformly random NN-lift belongs to Ω¯\bar{\Omega} with high probability. Throughout this paper, we fix a simple base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}} whose minimum degree is at least 33, and denote its maximum degree by dmaxd_{\rm max}. Fix a constant 𝔠∈(0,1){\mathfrak{c}}\in(0,1) and set ℜ:=(𝔠/4)​logdmax−1​N.{\mathfrak{R}}:=({\mathfrak{c}}/4)\log_{d_{\rm max}-1}N. For notational simplicity, throughout the paper we write log⁡N\log N for logdmax−1⁡N\log_{d_{\rm max}-1}N.

Definition 1.1.

Given a base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, let Ω¯⊂𝖦N​(ℋ)\bar{\Omega}\subset{\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}) denote the set of graphs that are tree-like up to radius ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} in the following sense:

  • •

    the radius-ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} neighborhood of every vertex contains at most one cycle;

  • •

    the number of vertices whose radius-ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} neighborhoods contain a cycle is at most N𝔠N^{{\mathfrak{c}}}.

Our main result is a quantitative local law for random lifts, stated precisely in Theorem 4.2. The quantitative estimates hold uniformly in the regular bulk and near all regular edges and regular cusps. Since the full statement requires several additional notion and parameters, we postpone its precise statement and first present the following simpler consequence in the regular bulk.

Theorem 1.2 (Bulk eigenvalue counting).

Fix any sufficiently large 𝔮∈ℕ+{\mathfrak{q}}\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be sampled uniformly from Ω¯\bar{\Omega}. For every sufficiently large N∈ℕ+N\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, with probability 1−O⁡(N−𝔮)1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}), the following holds:

Uniformly for all intervals II in the regular bulk that stay a fixed positive distance away from all edges, cusps, and singular energies and satisfy |I|⩾(log⁡N)C/N|I|\geqslant(\log N)^{C}/N for some sufficiently large constant C>0C>0, we have

#⁡{k:λk​(𝒢)∈I}=N​|ℍ|​∫Iρℋ​(E)​𝑑E+o⁡(N​|I|),\#\{k:\lambda_{k}({\mathcal{G}})\in I\}=N|{\mathbb{H}}|\int_{I}\rho_{{\mathcal{H}}}(E)\,\mathrm{d}E+o(N|I|),

where {λk​(𝒢)}\{\lambda_{k}({\mathcal{G}})\} are the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}, counted with multiplicity.

The quantitative local law Theorem 4.2 further implies delocalization of eigenvectors throughout the entire regular spectral regime. More precisely, away from the singular energies of the universal-cover spectrum, all normalized eigenvectors satisfy the following uniform ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} bound with high probability.

Theorem 1.3 (Eigenvector delocalization).

Fix any sufficiently large 𝔮∈ℕ+{\mathfrak{q}}\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be sampled uniformly from Ω¯\bar{\Omega}. For every sufficiently large N∈ℕ+N\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, with probability 1−O⁡(N−𝔮)1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}), the following holds:

For every normalized eigenvector uku_{k} of the adjacency matrix of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} whose eigenvalue λk​(𝒢)\lambda_{k}({\mathcal{G}}) stays a fixed positive distance away from the singular energies of the universal-cover spectrum, we have

|uk|∞⩽(log⁡N)CN,|u_{k}|_{\infty}\leqslant\frac{(\log N)^{C}}{\sqrt{N}},

where C>0C>0 is a sufficiently large constant and |⋅|∞|\cdot|_{\infty} denotes the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} norm.

1.3 Key ideas, challenges, and new contributions

In Section 4, we present the overall architecture and main flow of the proof, which follows the classical bootstrap and continuation scheme for Green’s function local laws; at its core are the two key propositions stated in Section 4.3, which are proved in Section 5 and Section 6, respectively.

Our proof exploits the fact that random lifts are locally tree-like. Since Green’s functions on trees admit exact recursive descriptions, see Proposition 2.9, our basic strategy is to reduce the global resolvent problem to calculations on local tree-like neighborhoods. More precisely, we approximate the Green’s function near a given vertex, or pair of vertices, by that of a suitable local neighborhood, while replacing the exterior of the graph by effective boundary weights. In this way, the local geometry is retained and the distant environment enters only through the boundary conditions. The essential question is therefore how these boundary weights should be chosen.

Boundary self-energies and empirical approximation.

Localizing the graph removes the connections between the chosen neighborhood and its exterior. These missing connections must be accounted for, since the Green’s function of the isolated neighborhood does not capture the influence of the surrounding graph. A natural first choice is to complete each missing boundary edge by the corresponding truncated universal-cover branch. The motivation is that, for large NN, a random lift is locally modeled by the universal cover of the base graph. On the universal cover itself, if one first localizes to a finite neighborhood and then attaches back the missing branches of the appropriate types, one exactly reconstructs the original universal-cover tree. Thus the corresponding universal-cover branches provide the most natural boundary completion for the localized finite graph. See Figure 3.

We denote the set of oriented edges of the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}} by E→ℋ\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}. Hence, the universal cover contains |E→ℋ||\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}| distinct types of branches, indexed by the directed edges of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. For e=(i,j)∈E→ℋe=(i,j)\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}, this branch, denoted by 𝒴e{\mathcal{Y}}_{e}, is rooted at a vertex of type jj, with the branch leading back to type ii removed. Its root Green’s function is denoted by me​(z)m_{e}(z), and attaching it along a missing edge of type ee contributes the boundary self-energy me​(z)m_{e}(z). For convenience, we will also write mi​jm_{ij} in place of mem_{e} when e=(i,j)e=(i,j), especially when the quantity appears as a subscript. The recursive structure of these branches gives the directed-edge Dyson equation

−1mi​j​(z)=z+∑k∼j,k≠imj​k​(z).-\frac{1}{m_{ij}(z)}=z+\sum_{k\sim j,k\neq i}m_{jk}(z).\vskip-5.69054pt (1.2)

Although these deterministic weights give the correct limiting boundary condition, replacing the exterior directly by them is not sufficient for the improvement argument near regular edges and cusps. In these regions, the Dyson equation becomes unstable, so a small error in the equation can produce a substantially larger deviation of its solution. A direct comparison with the deterministic boundary condition does not separate this collective deviation from the local fluctuations that can be reduced by averaging. Following the principle introduced by Huang and Yau in [42], we therefore first approximate the exterior using empirical boundary weights computed from the same graph. See Figure 3. The resulting comparison retains the collective fluctuation in the boundary condition and allows us to derive a self-consistent equation for it. Only after controlling this equation do we replace the empirical weights by the deterministic solution m⁡(z)m(z).

Choosing the empirical boundary weights.

The first difficulty is to identify empirical quantities that are compatible with both the tree recursion and the resolvent estimates. In the regular setting, Huang and Yau use an average of vertex-deleted Green’s function entries [42]. A direct use of such quantities in the present setting would require control of additional operators obtained by deleting vertices. This control cannot be inferred merely from boundedness of the original Green’s function. Indeed, deleting a vertex changes the boundary conditions and the spectrum of the auxiliary operator. Its Green’s function may consequently become large near an eigenvalue of the modified operator, even when the original Green’s function remains bounded at the same energy. Thus the use of vertex-deleted observables introduces spectral regularity questions that are not part of the original problem. This consideration also guides the graph operations throughout our analysis: we carefully avoid deleting vertices, since doing so could introduce artificial singularities that are difficult to control. In particular, the localization and switching procedures developed later are designed to preserve all vertices while modifying their connections, thereby avoiding the need for separate spectral estimates on vertex-deleted operators.

We instead construct the empirical weights entirely from Green’s function entries of the unmodified graph.

Definition 1.4 (Empirical vertex and directed-edge quantities).

For each vertex type i∈ℍi\in{\mathbb{H}}, define

Qver​(z):=(Qi​(z))i∈ℍ,Qi​(z):=1N​∑x∈𝔾,π⁡(x)=iGx​x​(z).Q^{\rm ver}(z):=(Q_{i}(z))_{i\in{\mathbb{H}}},\qquad Q_{i}(z):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in{\mathbb{G}},\pi(x)=i}G_{xx}(z).\vskip-5.69054pt (1.3)

For a directed edge e=(i,j)∈E→ℋe=(i,j)\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}} and a vertex xx with π⁡(x)=i\pi(x)=i, let xex_{e} denote the unique neighbor of xx corresponding to the lift of ee. Define

p⁡(z):=(pe​(z))e∈E→ℋ,pe​(z):=1N​∑x∈𝔾,π⁡(x)=iGx​xe​(z).p(z):=(p_{e}(z))_{e\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}},\qquad p_{e}(z):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x\in{\mathbb{G}},\pi(x)=i}G_{xx_{e}}(z).\vskip-5.69054pt (1.4)

The empirical directed-edge weights are

Q⁡(z):=(Qe​(z))e∈E→ℋ,Qe​(z):=−pe​(z)Qt⁡(e)​(z),Q(z):=(Q_{e}(z))_{e\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}},\qquad Q_{e}(z):=-\frac{p_{e}(z)}{Q_{t(e)}(z)},\vskip-11.38109pt (1.5)

where t⁡(e)t(e) denotes the initial vertex of ee.

This choice is motivated by the corresponding identity on the universal cover. Let GG be the Green’s function of the universal cover tree. For adjacent vertices x,yx,y with directed-edge type ee, we have Gx​y​(z)=−me​(z)​Gx​x​(z);G_{xy}(z)=-m_{e}(z)G_{xx}(z); see (2.14). Thus Qe=−pe/Qt⁡(e)Q_{e}=-p_{e}/Q_{t(e)} is the empirical analogue of the deterministic branch Green’s function mem_{e}.

An important advantage of this definition is that the empirical quantities satisfy an exact vertex–edge relation. Averaging the diagonal entries of (A−z)​G=I(A-z)G=I over vertices of type ii gives

1+z​Qi=∑j∼ipi​j.1+zQ_{i}=\sum_{j\sim i}p_{ij}.\vskip-14.22636pt (1.6)

Substituting pe=−Qt⁡(e)​Qep_{e}=-Q_{t(e)}Q_{e}, we obtain

−1Qi=z+∑j∼iQi​j.-\frac{1}{Q_{i}}=z+\sum_{j\sim i}Q_{ij}.\vskip-5.69054pt (1.7)

Hence the empirical vertex quantities are reconstructed from the empirical edge weights in exactly the same way as the corresponding Green’s functions on the universal cover. No additional error is introduced at this stage.

However, the directed-edge Dyson equation is only approximately satisfied. For a vector of nonzero boundary weights q=(qe)e∈E→ℋq=(q_{e})_{e\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}}, we measure its defect by the Dyson residual

R⁡(q,z)=(Re​(q,z))e∈E→ℋ,Ri​j​(q,z):=−1qi​j−z−∑k∼j,k≠iqj​k.R(q,z)=(R_{e}(q,z))_{e\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}},\qquad R_{ij}(q,z):=-\frac{1}{q_{ij}}-z-\sum_{k\sim j,k\neq i}q_{jk}.\vskip-5.69054pt (1.8)

Since R⁡(m,z)=0R(m,z)=0 where mm is the solution in (1.2), quantitative control of this residual, together with stability and the appropriate a priori control, provides estimates for the difference between QQ and mm. In this sense, the Dyson residual is the natural quantity that measures the deviation of QQ from the deterministic solution mm throughout the entire regular spectral regime: in the bulk, near regular edges, and near regular cusps. The only difference between these regimes lies in the stability with which a bound on R⁡(Q,z)R(Q,z) can be converted into a bound on Q−mQ-m.

Deterministic stability of the Dyson equation.

The spectral properties of the universal cover tree are governed by the directed-edge Dyson equation (1.2). Unlike the scalar equation in the regular case, this equation is vector-valued and involves the generally non-symmetric non-backtracking matrix BℋB_{{\mathcal{H}}} of the base graph. Our analysis therefore requires a detailed understanding of this equation, including the spectral decomposition of its solution m⁡(z)m(z), its boundedness, regularity, and singular behavior, as well as the quantitative stability of the equation, which allows us to convert bounds on the Dyson residual R⁡(Q,z)R(Q,z) into estimates for Q−mQ-m. The necessary theory was developed in our preceding work [41]; see Section 2.1.1 for details.

Anisotropic propagation and elliptic neighborhoods.

Another main difficulty comes from the loss of homogeneity of the universal cover. On a regular tree, Green’s function propagation along a path is governed by the same factor at every step. Consequently, vertices at a common distance from the root have comparable influence on its Green’s function. For a general base graph, the propagation factor depends on the directed-edge type. Products along paths of the same length can therefore differ exponentially in that length. An ordinary graph-distance sphere need not provide a balanced boundary for the averaging argument: a small collection of directions may carry a disproportionately large part of the contribution.

To address this problem, we replace ordinary balls by elliptic neighborhoods adapted to Green’s function propagation. Their construction uses Perron–Frobenius normalized path weights associated with the weighted non-backtracking operator. Unlike the unnormalized products of the mem_{e}, these weights decrease along each path, and their squares satisfy a conservation relation under branching. We stop a path when its normalized weight falls below a prescribed threshold, of order 2−ℓ2^{-\ell}, rather than when it reaches a prescribed graph distance. The resulting boundary is balanced in terms of propagation weights. This gives uniform control of root-to-boundary contributions and of the boundary sums appearing in the resolvent comparison. See Definition 2.16 and Proposition 2.18 for details.

Woodbury-based resolvent comparison.

A further simplification in our argument is that we organize the resolvent computations systematically through the Woodbury formula; see section 5.1 for details. Since the switchings and local modifications that appear in the proof are finite-rank perturbations, the Woodbury formula gives direct and transparent expressions for the corresponding changes of the Green’s function. This allows many resolvent comparisons to be treated within a single framework and avoids repeated Schur-complement expansions. As a result, the main estimates and cancellations become considerably more explicit, and the overall proof is substantially shorter and cleaner.

2 Tree-like Graphs

Recall the constants 0<𝔠<10<{\mathfrak{c}}<1 and ℜ=(𝔠/4)​log⁡N{\mathfrak{R}}=({\mathfrak{c}}/4)\log N. The following proposition is the basic geometric input for our spectral analysis. It shows that a uniformly random NN-lift belongs, with high probability, to the class Ω¯\bar{\Omega} of radius-ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} tree-like graphs introduced in Definition 1.1. Thus, the local law established in this paper on Ω¯\bar{\Omega} describes the spectral behavior of a typical random lift.

Proposition 2.1.

Let ℋ{\mathcal{H}} be a base graph with minimum degree at least three. For all sufficiently large NN, a uniformly random NN-lift 𝒢∈𝖦N​(ℋ){\mathcal{G}}\in{\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}) satisfies

ℙ⁡(𝒢∉Ω¯)≲N−(1−𝔠).\mathbb{P}\bigl({\mathcal{G}}\notin\bar{\Omega}\bigr)\lesssim N^{-(1-{\mathfrak{c}})}. (2.1)
Proof.

By [18, Lemma 27], the probability that every radius-ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} neighborhood in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} contains at most one cycle is at least 1−O⁡((dmax−1)4​ℜ/N)=1−O⁡(N−(1−𝔠)).1-\OO((d_{\rm max}-1)^{4{\mathfrak{R}}}/N)=1-\OO(N^{-(1-{\mathfrak{c}})}). Moreover, a slight adaptation of the argument proving [15, Proposition 4.1, (4.3)] to the permutation model of random lifts gives

ℙ⁡(|{x∈𝔾:ℬℜ​(x,𝒢)​ contains a cycle}|>(dmax−1)4​ℜ)≲N−(1−𝔠).\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\left\{x\in{\mathbb{G}}:{\mathcal{B}}_{{\mathfrak{R}}}(x,{\mathcal{G}})\text{ contains a cycle}\right\}\right|>(d_{\rm max}-1)^{4{\mathfrak{R}}}\right)\lesssim N^{-(1-{\mathfrak{c}})}.

Here, the configuration-model exploration in [15] is replaced by the corresponding sequential exposure of the permutations associated with the edges of the fixed base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. Combining the two estimates with a union bound yields (2.1). ∎

2.1 Quadratic vector equation and universal cover trees

In this section, we introduce the quadratic vector equation corresponding to the non-backtracking matrix of the base graph ℋ=(ℍ,Eℋ){\mathcal{H}}=({\mathbb{H}},E_{\mathcal{H}}) and list some properties of its solution. Then, we calculate the Green’s functions of the universal cover of the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}}.

2.1.1 The base graph and the quadratic vector equation

The adjacency matrix of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is denoted by H=(Hi​j)i,j∈ℍH=(H_{ij})_{i,j\in{\mathbb{H}}}, where Hi​j=1H_{ij}=1 if {i,j}∈Eℋ\{i,j\}\in E_{\mathcal{H}}; Hi​j=0H_{ij}=0 otherwise. In addition to the adjacency matrix, it is often convenient to encode the local structure of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} using the non-backtracking matrix (also called the Hashimoto matrix). Recall that E→ℋ\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}} denotes the set of directed edges of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. For a directed edge e=(i,j)e=(i,j), we write t⁡(e)=it(e)=i and h⁡(e)=jh(e)=j for its tail and head, respectively, and denote the reversed edge by e¯=(j,i).\bar{e}=(j,i). For oriented edges e,f∈E→ℋe,f\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}, we write e↝fe\rightsquigarrow f if ff follows ee without backtracking, that is, h⁡(e)=t⁡(f)h(e)=t(f) and f≠e¯.f\neq\bar{e}. For vertices i,j∈𝔾i,j\in{\mathbb{G}} where 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} is a lift of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, we use i↝ji\leadsto j to denote a non-backtracking path in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} from ii to jj. The non-backtracking matrix of ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is the |E→ℋ|×|E→ℋ||\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}|\times|\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}| matrix Bℋ=(Be​f)e,f∈E→ℋB_{{\mathcal{H}}}=(B_{ef})_{e,f\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}}, indexed by oriented edges, defined by Be​f=𝟏e↝f.B_{ef}=\mathbf{1}_{e\rightsquigarrow f}. Thus, BℋB_{{\mathcal{H}}} records the allowed one-step transitions of non-backtracking walks on ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. We shall also use the shorthand B:=BℋB:=B_{{\mathcal{H}}}.

For z∈ℂ+z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}, we consider a vector m⁡(z):=(me)e∈E→ℋ∈ℂ+E→ℋm(z):=(m_{e})_{e\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}}\in\mathbb{C}_{+}^{\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}} that satisfies the Dyson equation (1.2). The vector m⁡(z)m(z) provides an analytic description of the resolvent of the adjacency operator on the forward universal-cover branches, and plays a central role in the study of local spectral statistics and the limiting spectral distribution of random lifts of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. Besides mi​j​(z)m_{ij}(z), we also define

mver=(mi)i∈ℍ,where ​mi​(z):=−1z+∑j∼imi​j​(z),i∈ℍ.m^{\rm ver}=(m_{i})_{i\in{\mathbb{H}}},\qquad\mbox{where~}m_{i}(z):=\frac{-1}{z+\sum_{j\sim i}m_{ij}(z)},\qquad i\in{\mathbb{H}}. (2.2)

Some properties of the solution to the Dyson equation (1.2) are listed below. Before stating the results, we introduce the following notation. For a set II contained in ℝ\mathbb{R}, set ℂ+​(I):={z∈ℂ+:Re​z∈I}\mathbb{C}_{+}(I):=\{z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}:\mathrm{Re}z\in I\}. The first lemma shows the basic analytic properties of the solution to the Dyson equation, together with the structure of its singular set and regular spectral support.

Lemma 2.2 (Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.3 of [41]).

For every z∈ℂ+z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}, equation (1.2) has a unique solution m⁡(z)∈ℂ+E→ℋ,m(z)\in\mathbb{C}_{+}^{\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}}, and the map z↦m⁡(z)z\mapsto m(z) is analytic. There exists a finite set

𝒜ℋ:={τ∈ℝ:limη↓0|me​(τ+i​η)|=∞​for some e∈E→ℋ}\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}}:=\left\{\tau\in\mathbb{R}:\lim_{\eta\downarrow 0}|m_{e}(\tau+i\eta)|=\infty~\text{for some $e\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}$}\right\} (2.3)

such that the boundary value m⁡(τ):=limη↓0m⁡(τ+i​η)m(\tau):=\lim_{\eta\downarrow 0}m(\tau+\mathrm{i}\eta) exists and is finite for all τ∈ℝ∖𝒜ℋ\tau\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}}. For every e∈E→ℋe\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}, there exists a unique probability measure νe\nu_{e} such that

me​(z)=∫ℝνe​(d​τ)τ−z.m_{e}(z)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{\nu_{e}(\mathrm{d}\tau)}{\tau-z}.

The measure νe\nu_{e} admits the decomposition

νe​(d​τ)=ρe​(τ)​d​τ+∑τjwe,τj​δτj​(d​τ),\nu_{e}(\mathrm{d}\tau)=\rho_{e}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau+\sum_{\tau_{j}}w_{e,\tau_{j}}\,\delta_{\tau_{j}}(\mathrm{d}\tau),\vskip-8.53581pt

where τj∈𝒜ℋ\tau_{j}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}} is an atomic energy, we,τj>0w_{e,\tau_{j}}>0 are the corresponding atomic weights, and ρe\rho_{e} denotes the density of the absolutely continuous part. All these measures are supported in the compact interval [−Σ,Σ][-\Sigma,\Sigma] where Σ:=2​‖Bℋ‖∞1/2⩽2​dmax−1\Sigma:=2\|B_{\mathcal{H}}\|_{\infty}^{1/2}\leqslant 2\sqrt{d_{\rm max}-1}.

For a sufficiently small parameter δ>0\delta>0, we define the regular support away from the singular points by

𝒮δ:={τ∈ℝ:dist⁡(τ,𝒜ℋ)>δ​and​∑e∈E→ℋρe​(τ)>0}.\mathcal{S}_{\delta}:=\left\{\tau\in\mathbb{R}:\mathrm{dist}(\tau,\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}})>\delta~\mbox{and}~\sum_{e\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}}\rho_{e}(\tau)>0\right\}.

Then 𝒮δ\mathcal{S}_{\delta} is a finite union of bounded open intervals.

Remark 2.3.

The preceding theorem concerns the directed-edge quantities. By (2.2), the vertex Green functions mver=(mi)i∈ℍm^{\rm ver}=(m_{i})_{i\in{\mathbb{H}}}, and hence their associated spectral measures νi\nu_{i} and densities ρi\rho_{i}, are determined by the directed-edge Green functions (me)e∈E→ℋ(m_{e})_{e\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}}.

In particular, the density-of-states measure νℋ\nu_{{\mathcal{H}}} defined in (1.1) satisfies

νℋ=1|ℍ|​∑i∈ℍνi,ρℋ=1|ℍ|​∑i∈ℍρi.\nu_{{\mathcal{H}}}=\frac{1}{|{\mathbb{H}}|}\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{H}}}\nu_{i},\qquad\rho_{{\mathcal{H}}}=\frac{1}{|{\mathbb{H}}|}\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{H}}}\rho_{i}.

Moreover, it follows from Lemma 2.6 that

ρℋ​(τ)∼∑e∈E→ℋρe​(τ)\rho_{{\mathcal{H}}}(\tau)\sim\sum_{e\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}}\rho_{e}(\tau)

throughout the regular spectral region. Consequently, the vertex and directed-edge densities have the same positivity set, and the corresponding regularity and boundary properties of the vertex quantities follow from those of the directed-edge quantities.

Remark 2.4.

The purpose of introducing 𝒮δ\mathcal{S}_{\delta} is to exclude the singular points at which the solution blows up, since such blow-up destroys most of the regularity and stability properties required in the subsequent analysis. As δ\delta decreases to zero, the set 𝒮δ\mathcal{S}_{\delta} approaches the positive-density region of the absolutely continuous spectrum away from the singular points. Thus,ww a smaller choice of δ\delta retains a larger portion of the real line and, in this sense, yields a more precise description of the solution. On the other hand, every regular edge or cusp that does not coincide with an atomic singularity admits a neighborhood on which the solution remains uniformly bounded. Hence, by choosing δ\delta sufficiently small, removing the δ\delta-neighborhoods of the singular points does not exclude such regular edges or cusps.

Since the spectrum of an NN-lift need not be contained in 𝒮δ\mathcal{S}_{\delta}, while it is always contained in [−dmax,dmax][-d_{\max},d_{\max}], we introduce the larger spectral domain

ℐδ:={τ∈[−dmax,dmax]:dist⁡(τ,𝒜ℋ)⩾δ}.\mathcal{I}_{\delta}:=\left\{\tau\in[-d_{\max},d_{\max}]:\mathrm{dist}(\tau,\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{H}})\geqslant\delta\right\}.

Clearly, it follows that 𝒮δ⊂ℐδ\mathcal{S}_{\delta}\subset\mathcal{I}_{\delta}. All subsequent analysis in this paper will be carried out on the domain ℂ+​(ℐδ){\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}). Moreover, by Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.3 of [41], m⁡(z)m(z) is uniformly bounded on ℂ+​(ℐδ){\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}): supz∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)|m⁡(z)|2⩽Φδ<∞,\sup_{z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta})}|m(z)|_{2}\leqslant\Phi_{\delta}<\infty, where Φδ\Phi_{\delta} depends on the model parameters and δ\delta.

We next classify the regular spectral points according to the local structure of the support.

Definition 2.5 (Spectral regimes).

Fix the parameter δ>0\delta>0 as in Lemma 2.2. A point τ∈ℐδ\tau\in\mathcal{I}_{\delta} is called

  • •

    an off-support point if τ∈ℐδ∖𝒮δ¯.\tau\in\mathcal{I}_{\delta}\setminus\overline{\mathcal{S}_{\delta}}.

  • •

    a regular bulk point if τ∈𝒮δ\tau\in\mathcal{S}_{\delta};

  • •

    a regular edge if τ∈∂𝒮δ\tau\in\partial\mathcal{S}_{\delta}, ρℋ​(τ)=0\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\tau)=0, and τ\tau is the endpoint of exactly one connected component of 𝒮δ\mathcal{S}_{\delta}. We denote by 𝒮edge\mathcal{S}_{\rm edge} the set of all regular edges.

  • •

    a regular cusp if τ∈∂𝒮δ\tau\in\partial\mathcal{S}_{\delta}, ρℋ​(τ)=0\rho_{\mathcal{H}}(\tau)=0, and τ\tau is the common endpoint of two connected components of 𝒮δ\mathcal{S}_{\delta}. We denote by 𝒮cusp\mathcal{S}_{\rm cusp} the set of all regular cusps.

We next record the uniform bounds and regularity of the Dyson solution, together with the characteristic square-root and cubic-root behavior at regular edges and cusps. The proof of the following lemma is in the Appendix B.

Lemma 2.6 (Boundedness and regularity).

For every e∈E→ℋe\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}} and i∈ℍi\in{\mathbb{H}} and z=E+i​η∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z=E+i\eta\in\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}), we have

|me​(z)|∼|mi​(z)|∼11+|z|,Im​me​(z)∼Im​mi​(z)∼{|z−τ|1/2,z​ is close to a regular edge ​τ,E​ lies on the spectral side of ​τ,η|z−τ|1/2,z​ is close to a regular edge ​τ,E​ lies on the off-support side of ​τ,|z−τ|1/3,z​ is close to a regular cusp ​τ,(1+|z|)−1,z​ is in the stable bulk,η(1+|z|)2,z​ is in the stable off-support regime.|m_{e}(z)|\sim|m_{i}(z)|\sim\frac{1}{1+|z|},\quad{\mathrm{Im}}m_{e}(z)\sim{\mathrm{Im}}m_{i}(z)\sim\begin{cases}|z-\tau|^{1/2},&\begin{array}[]{l}z\text{ is close to a regular edge }\tau,\\[-2.84526pt] E\text{ lies on the spectral side of }\tau,\end{array}\\[11.38109pt] \dfrac{\eta}{|z-\tau|^{1/2}},&\begin{array}[]{l}z\text{ is close to a regular edge }\tau,\\[-2.84526pt] E\text{ lies on the off-support side of }\tau,\end{array}\\[14.22636pt] |z-\tau|^{1/3},&z\text{ is close to a regular cusp }\tau,\\[5.69054pt] (1+|z|)^{-1},&z\text{ is in the stable bulk},\\[5.69054pt] \dfrac{\eta}{(1+|z|)^{2}},&z\text{ is in the stable off-support regime}.\end{cases} (2.4)

Moreover, the solution me​(z)m_{e}(z) and density ρe​(τ)\rho_{e}(\tau) are uniformly α\alpha-Hölder continuous on ℂ+​(ℐδ)¯\overline{\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta})} and 𝒮δ\mathcal{S}_{\delta} respectively, where α\alpha is a finite positive exponent depending only on the model parameters.

We shall repeatedly encounter approximate solutions of the Dyson equation. For a vector of boundary weights q=(qe)e∈E→ℋq=(q_{e})_{e\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}} with nonzero entries, recall the Dyson residual R⁡(q,z)R(q,z) defined in (1.8).

Since R⁡(m⁡(z),z)=0R(m(z),z)=0, writing q⁡(z)=m⁡(z)+u⁡(z)q(z)=m(z)+u(z) and subtracting the Dyson equation (1.2) for mm yields the exact identity

(I−m2​B)​u=m2​R​(q,z)+u2q.(I-m^{2}B)u=m^{2}R(q,z)+\frac{u^{2}}{q}. (2.5)

Thus I−m2​BI-m^{2}B describes the linear stability of the Dyson equation, while the second term on the right-hand side of (2.5) becomes relevant precisely when the linear stability degenerates.

Away from the spectral singularities, the linear term is stable and a small Dyson residual directly implies that qq is close to mm. Near a regular edge or cusp, however, the inverse of I−m2​BI-m^{2}B becomes singular, and the quadratic and cubic structure of the Dyson equation provides the additional stability required to control the unstable direction. The following lemma collects these stability estimates.

Then, for zz sufficiently close to 00, provided that |∑i∈ℍσi​(qi​(z)−mi​(z))|⩽c0,\left|\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{H}}}\sigma_{i}\bigl(q_{i}(z)-m_{i}(z)\bigr)\right|\leqslant c_{0}, we have

    |q⁡(z)−m⁡(z)|∞≲|R⁡(q,z)|∞+|∑i∈ℍσi​(qi​(z)−mi​(z))|.|q(z)-m(z)|_{\infty}\lesssim|R(q,z)|_{\infty}+\left|\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{H}}}\sigma_{i}\bigl(q_{i}(z)-m_{i}(z)\bigr)\right|. (2.8)

    Regular edges and cusps. Let τ\tau be a regular edge or cusp, and let z=E+i​ηz=E+\mathrm{i}\eta be sufficiently close to τ\tau, with η<η0\eta<\eta_{0}. Assume further that there exists a continuous family (qt)η⩽t⩽η0(q_{t})_{\eta\leqslant t\leqslant\eta_{0}} satisfying qη=q⁡(z)q_{\eta}=q(z) and

    supη⩽t⩽η0|qt−m⁡(E+i​t)|∞⩽c0,supη⩽t⩽η0|R⁡(qt,E+i​t)|∞⩽ε.\sup_{\eta\leqslant t\leqslant\eta_{0}}|q_{t}-m(E+\mathrm{i}t)|_{\infty}\leqslant c_{0},\qquad\sup_{\eta\leqslant t\leqslant\eta_{0}}|R(q_{t},E+\mathrm{i}t)|_{\infty}\leqslant\varepsilon. (2.9)

    Then, for |z−τ||z-\tau| sufficiently small,

    |q⁡(z)−m⁡(z)|∞≲{ε(ε+|z−τ|)1/2,τ∈𝒮edge,ε(ε+|z−τ|)2/3,τ∈𝒮cusp.|q(z)-m(z)|_{\infty}\lesssim\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\varepsilon}{(\varepsilon+|z-\tau|)^{1/2}},&\tau\in\mathcal{S}_{\rm edge},\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle\frac{\varepsilon}{(\varepsilon+|z-\tau|)^{2/3}},&\tau\in\mathcal{S}_{\rm cusp}.\end{cases} (2.10)
Remark 2.8 (Selection of the branch).

The continuity assumption (2.9) in the edge and cusp regimes is used to select the branch of the Dyson equation. Indeed, near a regular edge or cusp the linearized Dyson operator becomes singular, and the corresponding nonlinear equation may have several local solution branches which coalesce at edges and cusps. Consequently, the pointwise assumptions |q−m⁡(z)|∞⩽c0|q-m(z)|_{\infty}\leqslant c_{0} and |R⁡(q,z)|∞⩽ε,|R(q,z)|_{\infty}\leqslant\varepsilon, do not by themselves guarantee that qq lies on the branch issued from the true solution m⁡(z)m(z): as zz approaches the edge or cusp, a different branch may enter any fixed c0c_{0}-neighborhood of m⁡(z)m(z).

The family (qt)η⩽t⩽η0(q_{t})_{\eta\leqslant t\leqslant\eta_{0}} rules out this ambiguity. The upper endpoint E+i​η0E+\mathrm{i}\eta_{0} is chosen in a uniformly stable region, where the solution close to m⁡(E+i​η0)m(E+\mathrm{i}\eta_{0}) is locally unique. The continuity of qtq_{t}, together with the uniform bound on its Dyson residual, then ensures that qtq_{t} follows the branch continuously connected to the true solution as tt decreases from η0\eta_{0} to η\eta. In the stable bulk no such condition is needed, since the linearized Dyson operator is uniformly invertible and hence already gives local uniqueness in a fixed neighborhood of mm.

2.1.2 Green’s function on universal cover trees

In this subsection, since the universal cover of the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}} is an infinite tree, we can explicitly compute its Green’s function.

In the remainder of the paper, we extend the quantities mi​j​(z)m_{ij}(z) to coverings of the base graph by interpreting the indices in terms of vertex types. Specifically, for adjacent vertices i,ji,j in the covering graph, we define

mi​j​(z):=mπ⁡(i)​π​(j)​(z)m_{ij}(z):=m_{\pi(i)\,\pi(j)}(z) (2.11)

where π\pi is the covering map. In other words, the value of mi​j​(z)m_{ij}(z) on the universal cover depends only on the types of ii and jj in the base graph.

For a given path γ=(i=i0,i1,…,iℓ=j),\gamma=(i=i_{0},i_{1},\ldots,i_{\ell}=j), we define its path weight by

ℳ⁡(γ,z):=∏k=0ℓ−1(−mik​ik+1​(z)),\mathcal{M}(\gamma;z):=\prod_{k=0}^{\ell-1}\bigl(-m_{i_{k}i_{k+1}}(z)\bigr), (2.12)

where mik​ik+1​(z)m_{i_{k}i_{k+1}}(z) denotes the Green function associated with the directed edge type of ik→ik+1i_{k}\to i_{k+1} in the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. For a path of length zero, we set ℳ⁡(γ,z)=1\mathcal{M}(\gamma;z)=1.

In particular, if 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} is a tree, then any two vertices i,j∈𝔾i,j\in{\mathbb{G}} are connected by a unique simple path, denoted by [i,j]=(i=i0,i1,…,iℓ=j).[i,j]=(i=i_{0},i_{1},\ldots,i_{\ell}=j). We therefore define

ℳ𝒢​(i,j,z):=ℳ⁡([i,j],z)=∏k=0ℓ−1(−mik​ik+1​(z)).\mathcal{M}_{{\mathcal{G}}}(i,j;z):=\mathcal{M}([i,j];z)=\prod_{k=0}^{\ell-1}\bigl(-m_{i_{k}i_{k+1}}(z)\bigr). (2.13)

When the underlying tree is clear from the context, we simply write ℳ⁡(i,j,z)\mathcal{M}(i,j;z).

Proposition 2.9.

Let 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} be the universal cover of the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. For all z∈ℂ+z\in\mathbb{C}^{+} and i,j∈𝕏i,j\in{\mathbb{X}}, the Green’s function of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} is

Gi​j​(z)=mi​(z)​ℳ𝒳​(i,j,z).G_{ij}(z)=m_{i}(z)\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{X}}(i,j;z). (2.14)

Fix a directed edge e=(k,l)∈ℍe=(k,l)\in{\mathbb{H}}. Let 𝒴e{\mathcal{Y}}_{e} be the truncated universal cover rooted at vertex oo of type ll, obtained by deleting the edge adjacent to oo of type {l,k}\{l,k\}. For every i∈𝕐ei\in\mathbb{Y}_{e}, we have

Go​i​(z)=me​(z)​ℳ𝒴e​(o,i,z).G_{oi}(z)=m_{e}(z)\mathcal{M}_{{\mathcal{Y}}_{e}}(o,i;z). (2.15)

In particular, Go​o​(z)=me​(z)G_{oo}(z)=m_{e}(z).

Proof.

For an oriented edge (x,y)(x,y) of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, by the same argument in [15, Proof of Proposition 5.1], the Schur complement formula (A.2) together with the Dyson equation (1.2) gives Gx​x=mxG_{xx}=m_{x} and Gx​y=−mx​y​Gx​x.G_{xy}=-m_{xy}G_{xx}. Iterating the same identity along the unique path [i,j]=(i=i0,i1,…,iℓ=j)[i,j]=(i=i_{0},i_{1},\ldots,i_{\ell}=j) in 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, we obtain

Gi​j=mi​∏r=0ℓ−1(−mir​ir+1)=mi​ℳ𝒳​(i,j),G_{ij}=m_{i}\prod_{r=0}^{\ell-1}(-m_{i_{r}i_{r+1}})=m_{i}{\mathcal{M}}_{{\mathcal{X}}}(i,j),

which proves (2.14).

For 𝒴e{\mathcal{Y}}_{e}, the same argument applies verbatim. By the Schur complement formula and the directed-edge Dyson equation, the removal of the branch of type {l,k}\{l,k\} gives Go​o=me.G_{oo}=m_{e}. Iterating the identity Gx​y=−mx​y​Gx​xG_{xy}=-m_{xy}G_{xx} along the unique path from oo to i∈𝕐ei\in\mathbb{Y}_{e} therefore yields Go​i=me​ℳ𝒴e​(o,i),G_{oi}=m_{e}\mathcal{M}_{{\mathcal{Y}}_{e}}(o,i), which proves (2.15). ∎

Next we introduce two types of weighted non-backtracking matrices. For z∈ℂ+z\in\mathbb{C}^{+}, define

M⁡(z):=Bℋ​diag⁡(me​(z)2)e∈E→ℋ,M~​(z):=Bℋ​diag⁡(|me​(z)|2)e∈E→ℋ.M(z):=B_{\mathcal{H}}\operatorname{diag}\bigl(m_{e}(z)^{2}\bigr)_{e\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}},\qquad\widetilde{M}(z):=B_{\mathcal{H}}\operatorname{diag}\bigl(|m_{e}(z)|^{2}\bigr)_{e\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}}.

More precisely,

Me​f(z)=𝟏{e↝f}mf(z)2,M~e​f(z)=𝟏{e↝f}|mf(z)|2.M_{ef}(z)=\mathbf{1}_{\{e\rightsquigarrow f\}}m_{f}(z)^{2},\qquad\widetilde{M}_{ef}(z)=\mathbf{1}_{\{e\rightsquigarrow f\}}|m_{f}(z)|^{2}.

The matrices M⁡(z)M(z) and M~​(z)\widetilde{M}(z) provide a finite-dimensional way to encode weighted non-backtracking propagation over long distances in the universal cover or a large lift of the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. Indeed, for every ℓ⩾1\ell\geqslant 1,

(Mℓ​(z))e​f=∑e=e0↝e1↝⋯↝eℓ=f∏r=1ℓmer​(z)2.\bigl(M^{\ell}(z)\bigr)_{ef}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e=e_{0}\rightsquigarrow e_{1}\rightsquigarrow\cdots\rightsquigarrow e_{\ell}=f\end{subarray}}~\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}m_{e_{r}}(z)^{2}.

Consequently, (Mℓ​(z))e​f\bigl(M^{\ell}(z)\bigr)_{ef} is the sum of the weights of all ℓ\ell-step non-backtracking walks in the universal cover that start from a fixed directed edge of type ee and end at a directed edge of type ff. The weight of such a walk is ∏r=1ℓmer​(z)2;\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}m_{e_{r}}(z)^{2}; that is, every directed edge entered after the initial edge contributes the factor mer​(z)2m_{e_{r}}(z)^{2}. The same interpretation applies to non-backtracking walks in a large lift of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}.

Likewise,

(M~ℓ​(z))e​f=∑e=e0↝e1↝⋯↝eℓ=f∏r=1ℓ|mer​(z)|2,\bigl(\widetilde{M}^{\ell}(z)\bigr)_{ef}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e=e_{0}\rightsquigarrow e_{1}\rightsquigarrow\cdots\rightsquigarrow e_{\ell}=f\end{subarray}}~\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}|m_{e_{r}}(z)|^{2}, (2.16)

and therefore

|(Mℓ​(z))e​f|⩽(M~ℓ​(z))e​f.\left|\bigl(M^{\ell}(z)\bigr)_{ef}\right|\leqslant\bigl(\widetilde{M}^{\ell}(z)\bigr)_{ef}.

Thus, although MM and M~\widetilde{M} are indexed only by the directed edges of the base graph, their powers encode the contributions of non-backtracking walks over arbitrarily long distances in the universal cover or in a large lift. The matrix MℓM^{\ell} retains the complex phases and possible cancellations among the walk weights, whereas M~ℓ\widetilde{M}^{\ell} provides a nonnegative majorant suitable for long-range decay and summability estimates.

The largest eigenvalue λ1​(z)\lambda_{1}(z) of M~​(z)\widetilde{M}(z) is positive and real. Moreover, we have

at distance ℓ\ell corresponds to a unique ℓ\ell-step non-backtracking walk e=e0↝e1↝⋯↝eℓe=e_{0}\rightsquigarrow e_{1}\rightsquigarrow\cdots\rightsquigarrow e_{\ell}, and its squared Green function weight is |me​(z)|2​∏r=1ℓ|mer​(z)|2.|m_{e}(z)|^{2}\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}|m_{e_{r}}(z)|^{2}.

We next introduce a normalized version of the path weight which is adapted to the Perron–Frobenius structure of the weighted non-backtracking matrix M~​(z)\widetilde{M}(z). Recall from Proposition 2.10 that

M~​(z)​𝒗​(z)=λ1​(z)​𝒗​(z),where ​𝒗​(z)=(ve​(z))e∈E→ℋ>0​and​ve​(z)∼vf​(z).\widetilde{M}(z)\bm{v}(z)=\lambda_{1}(z)\bm{v}(z),\qquad\mbox{where~}\bm{v}(z)=(v_{e}(z))_{e\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}}>0~\mbox{and}~v_{e}(z)\sim v_{f}(z).
Definition 2.11 (PF-normalized path weight).

For k⩾1k\geqslant 1, let γ=(x0,x1,…,xk)\gamma=(x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}) be a simple path in a lift of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, and let es=(π⁡(xs−1),π⁡(xs))∈E→ℋ.e_{s}=\bigl(\pi(x_{s-1}),\pi(x_{s})\bigr)\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}. Define

ℳPF(γ;z):=λ1(z)−|γ|/2ℳ(γ;z)vek​(z)ve1​(z).\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z):=\lambda_{1}(z)^{-|\gamma|/2}\mathcal{M}(\gamma;z)\sqrt{\frac{v_{e_{k}}(z)}{v_{e_{1}}(z)}}. (2.17)

For the trivial path consisting of a single vertex, we set ℳPF​(γ,z)=1.\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)=1.

Then, it follows from ve∼vfv_{e}\sim v_{f} and λ1⩽1\lambda_{1}\leqslant 1 that

|ℳ⁡(γ,z)|≲|ℳPF​(γ,z)|.\left|\mathcal{M}(\gamma;z)\right|\lesssim\left|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)\right|. (2.18)

The normalization in (2.17) is useful for the following reasons. The factors mem_{e} appearing in the original path weight are not necessarily bounded in modulus by one; in particular, it may happen that |me|>1|m_{e}|>1. Thus the weight along a fixed path may fluctuate locally, and an endpoint condition does not by itself give a monotone stopping rule. The PF-normalized weight gives a stronger local structure. Indeed, if γ\gamma ends with a directed edge of type ee and γ​f\gamma f denotes an admissible non-backtracking extension of γ\gamma by an edge of type ff, then

|ℳPF​(γ​f,z)||ℳPF​(γ,z)|=λ1(z)−1/2|mf(z)|vf​(z)ve​(z).\frac{|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma f;z)|}{|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|}=\lambda_{1}(z)^{-1/2}|m_{f}(z)|\sqrt{\frac{v_{f}(z)}{v_{e}(z)}}. (2.19)

By the Perron–Frobenius equation, we have

∑f:e↝f|mf(z)|2vf​(z)ve​(z)=λ1(z)⟹∑f:e↝f|ℳPF​(γ​f,z)|2|ℳPF​(γ,z)|2=1.\sum_{f:\,e\rightsquigarrow f}|m_{f}(z)|^{2}\frac{v_{f}(z)}{v_{e}(z)}=\lambda_{1}(z)\Longrightarrow\sum_{f:e\rightsquigarrow f}\frac{|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma f;z)|^{2}}{|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|^{2}}=1. (2.20)

Hence |ℳPF||\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}| is non-increasing along every fixed non-backtracking path. Moreover, (2.20) shows that the squared PF-normalized weights define a conserved mass on the unfolded non-backtracking path tree.

Proposition 2.12.

There exists a constant β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), depending only on the model parameters, such that for every simple path γ\gamma from ii to jj in a lift 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} of the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}},

|ℳPF​(γ,z)|≲β|γ|⩽βdist𝒢​(i,j),z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ).\left|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)\right|\lesssim\beta^{|\gamma|}\leqslant\beta^{\mathrm{dist}_{\mathcal{G}}(i,j)},\qquad z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}).

2.2 Tree extension and Elliptic neighborhood

2.2.1 Tree extension

Definition 2.13 (Missing type).

Let 𝒢^\widehat{{\mathcal{G}}} be a lift of the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}} with covering map π:𝒢^→ℋ\pi:\widehat{{\mathcal{G}}}\to{\mathcal{H}}, and let 𝒢⊂𝒢^{\mathcal{G}}\subset\widehat{{\mathcal{G}}} be a subgraph. We use the restriction of π\pi to 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} as its type map. For v∈𝔾v\in{\mathbb{G}}, denote the set of directed edge types emanating from π⁡(v)\pi(v) by

E→ℋ​(π⁡(v)):={e∈E→ℋ:tail⁡(e)=π⁡(v)},\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}(\pi(v)):=\bigl\{e\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}:\operatorname{tail}(e)=\pi(v)\bigr\},

and the set of directed edge types present at vv in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} by

E→𝒢(v):={π(e):e∈E→𝒢,tail(e)=v}⊂E→ℋ(π(v)).\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{G}}}(v):=\bigl\{\pi(e):e\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{G}}},\ \operatorname{tail}(e)=v\bigr\}\subset\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}(\pi(v)).

The set of missing types at vv is

ℳ𝒢​(v):=E→ℋ​(π⁡(v))∖E→𝒢​(v).\mathscr{M}_{{\mathcal{G}}}(v):=\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}(\pi(v))\setminus\vec{E}_{\mathcal{G}}(v).
Definition 2.14 (Tree extension).

Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be a subgraph of a lift of the base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, and let v∈𝔾v\in{\mathbb{G}}. If ℳ𝒢​(v)≠∅,\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{G}}(v)\neq\varnothing, then, for each directed missing edge type e∈ℳ𝒢​(v),e\in\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{G}}(v), we attach to vv a fresh copy of the truncated universal cover branch 𝒴e{\mathcal{Y}}_{e} by joining vv to the root of 𝒴e{\mathcal{Y}}_{e} with an edge of directed type ee. All the attached copies of 𝒴e{\mathcal{Y}}_{e} are taken to be mutually disjoint apart from their attachment to vv. By performing the above operation simultaneously at every vertex v∈𝔾v\in{\mathbb{G}}, we obtain the tree extension of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}, denoted by TE⁡(𝒢).\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{G}}).

The next proposition shows that the Green’s function of the tree extension of a graph with at most one cycle can be bounded by that of the universal cover.

Proposition 2.15 (Green’s function estimates for tree extensions).

Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be a connected subgraph of a lift of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, containing at most one cycle. Then for all z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}^{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) and all i,j∈𝔾i,j\in{\mathbb{G}},

|Gi​j(TE(𝒢),z)|≲maxγ:i↝j|ℳ(γ;z)|≲βdist𝒢​(i,j),|ImGi​j(TE(𝒢),z)|≲|Immver|∞,\displaystyle\left|G_{ij}\bigl(\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{G}}),z\bigr)\right|\lesssim\max_{\gamma:i\leadsto j}|{\mathcal{M}}(\gamma;z)|\lesssim\beta^{\mathrm{dist}_{{\mathcal{G}}}(i,j)},\qquad\left|{\mathrm{Im}}G_{ij}\bigl(\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{G}}),z\bigr)\right|\lesssim|\im m^{\rm ver}|_{\infty}, (2.23)

where β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) is the parameter defined in Proposition 2.12.

2.2.2 Elliptic neighborhoods

We now define the elliptic neighborhood. Let Γr​(o,x)\Gamma_{r}(o,x) denote the set of simple paths from oo to xx contained in ℬr​(o,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}}) with r=ℜ/50r={\mathfrak{R}}/50. Hence ℬr{\mathcal{B}}_{r} is a tree-like neighborhood by Definition 1.1, which contains at most one cycle.

Definition 2.16 (Elliptic neighborhood).

For z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) and ℓ∼log4⁡log⁡N\ell\sim\log_{4}\log N, define

ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z):={x∈ℬr​(o,𝒢): there exists ​γ∈Γr​(o,x)​ such that ​|ℳPF​(γ,z)|⩾2−ℓ}.{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z):=\left\{x\in{\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}}):\text{ there exists }\gamma\in\Gamma_{r}(o,x)\text{ such that }|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|\geqslant 2^{-\ell}\right\}. (2.24)

By |ℳPF||{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm PF}| is non-increasing, if a path γ\gamma is admissible in (2.24), then every prefix path of γ\gamma is admissible as well. In particular, ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z){\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z) is connected.

Remark 2.17 (Locality of the elliptic neighborhood).

The definition (2.24) is insensitive to changes strictly outside the elliptic neighborhood. More precisely, let 𝒯:=ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z).{\mathcal{T}}:={\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z). By Definition 2.16, 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} depends only on the edge types along admissible paths. Therefore, changing edges entirely outside 𝒯{\mathcal{T}}, or rewiring edges between 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} and its exterior while preserving their edge types, does not affect the elliptic neighborhood.

We next collect the main estimates for the elliptic neighborhood. To formulate them conveniently, we first introduce the elliptic level of a vertex. For x∈ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)x\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z), define its elliptic level by

ℓx:=min⁡{k⩾0:x∈ℬkell​(o,𝒢,z)}.\ell_{x}:=\min\left\{k\geqslant 0:x\in{\mathcal{B}}_{k}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z)\right\}. (2.25)
Proposition 2.18 (Estimates for the elliptic neighborhood).

Let z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) and ℓ=O⁡(log⁡log⁡N)\ell=\OO(\log\log N). Then the following estimates hold.

  • (i)

    The outer vertex boundary of the elliptic neighborhood satisfies

    |∂ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)|∼4ℓ.\left|\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z)\right|\sim 4^{\ell}. (2.26)
  • (ii)

    For every j∈ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)j\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z),

    ∑y∈∂ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)|Gj​y​(TE⁡(ℬr​(o,𝒢)),z)|2≲1.\sum_{y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z)}|G_{jy}(\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}})),z)|^{2}\lesssim 1. (2.27)
  • (iii)

    For every j∈ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)j\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z),

    ∑y∈ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)|Gj​y​(TE⁡(ℬr​(o,𝒢)),z)|2≲ℓ.\sum_{y\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z)}|G_{jy}(\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}})),z)|^{2}\lesssim\ell. (2.28)
  • (iv)

    If j∈ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)j\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z) has elliptic level ℓj\ell_{j}, then

    ∑y∈∂ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)|Gj​y​(TE⁡(ℬr​(o,𝒢)),z)|≲(1+ℓj)​2ℓ−ℓj.\sum_{y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z)}|G_{jy}(\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}})),z)|\lesssim(1+\ell_{j})2^{\ell-\ell_{j}}. (2.29)
  • (v)

    If i,j∈ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)i,j\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z) have elliptic levels ℓi\ell_{i} and ℓj\ell_{j}, respectively, then

    ∑y∈∂ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z)|Gi​y​(TE⁡(ℬr​(o,𝒢)),z)|​|Gy​j​(TE⁡(ℬr​(o,𝒢)),z)|≲(1+|ℓi−ℓj|)​2−|ℓi−ℓj|.\sum_{y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z)}|G_{iy}(\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}})),z)|\,|G_{yj}(\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}})),z)|\lesssim\bigl(1+|\ell_{i}-\ell_{j}|\bigr)2^{-|\ell_{i}-\ell_{j}|}. (2.30)
Proof.

For simplicity, write Gi​j:=Gi​j​(TE⁡(ℬr​(o,𝒢)),z),G_{ij}:=G_{ij}(\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}})),z), and suppress (o,𝒢,z)(o,{\mathcal{G}};z) in the notation ℬℓell{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}. By O⁡(log4⁡log⁡N)=ℓ≪r=O⁡(log⁡N)\OO(\log_{4}\log N)=\ell\ll r=\OO(\log N), all relevant stopping paths and boundary vertices lie inside ℬr​(o,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}}).

Since ℬr​(o,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}}) contains at most one cycle, there are at most two simple paths between any two vertices. Thus Proposition 2.15 and (2.18) give

|Gi​j|≲maxγ:i→j|ℳPF(γ;z)|,|G_{ij}|\lesssim\max_{\gamma:i\to j}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|, (2.31)

where the maximum is over simple paths in ℬr​(o,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}}). Throughout the proof, x↝yx\leadsto y denotes a path attaining this maximum.

We shall use the multiplicative comparison

|ℳPF​(γ1​γ2,z)|∼|ℳPF​(γ1,z)​ℳPF​(γ2,z)||\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2};z)|\sim|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma_{1};z)\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma_{2};z)|

whenever γ1\gamma_{1} and γ2\gamma_{2} can be joined to form a simple path. Furthermore, for x,y∈ℬℓellx,y\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}, we have

|ℳPF(x↝y;z)|≲2−|ℓx−ℓy|.|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(x\leadsto y;z)|\lesssim 2^{-|\ell_{x}-\ell_{y}|}. (2.32)

The tree case. We first assume that ℬr​(o,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}}) is a tree. All path-mass calculations are performed on its full tree extension TE​(ℬr​(o,𝒢))\mathrm{TE}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(o,{\mathcal{G}})).

Let 𝒜1​(o)\mathscr{A}_{1}(o) denote the one-step paths starting from oo. For every nonempty path γ\gamma starting from oo, define

μ⁡(γ):=Zo​(z)−1​|ℳPF​(γ,z)|2,Zo​(z):=∑γ∈𝒜1​(o)|ℳPF​(γ,z)|2.\mu(\gamma):=Z_{o}(z)^{-1}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|^{2},\qquad Z_{o}(z):=\sum_{\gamma\in\mathscr{A}_{1}(o)}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|^{2}. (2.33)

Set μ⁡((o)):=1\mu((o)):=1 for the trivial path. For any other starting vertex jj, define ZjZ_{j} and μj\mu_{j} analogously.

The PF equation and the uniform comparison of the cavity moduli and PF eigenvector entries give λ1​(z)∼|me​(z)|2\lambda_{1}(z)\sim|m_{e}(z)|^{2}. Consequently, the one-step PF weights have modulus comparable to one, and Zj∼1Z_{j}\sim 1 uniformly in jj. For a nonempty path γ\gamma ending with edge type ee,

|ℳPF​(γ​f,z)|2|ℳPF​(γ,z)|2=pe​f​(z),c⩽pe​f​(z)⩽1−c.\frac{|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma f;z)|^{2}}{|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|^{2}}=p_{ef}(z),\qquad c\leqslant p_{ef}(z)\leqslant 1-c.

Here the lower bound follows from (2.21), while the upper bound uses the minimum-degree assumption and ∑fpe​f=1\sum_{f}p_{ef}=1.

Thus the PF identity (2.20) gives

∑γ′∈Ch⁡(γ)μj​(γ′)=μj​(γ),\sum_{\gamma^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Ch}(\gamma)}\mu_{j}(\gamma^{\prime})=\mu_{j}(\gamma),

where Ch⁡(γ)\operatorname{Ch}(\gamma) denotes the set of all admissible non-backtracking one-step extensions of γ\gamma. A family is called prefix-free if no member is a proper prefix of another member. For every such family 𝒫\mathscr{P} starting from jj, mass conservation implies

∑γ∈𝒫μj​(γ)⩽1,∑γ∈𝒫|ℳPF​(γ,z)|2≲1.\sum_{\gamma\in\mathscr{P}}\mu_{j}(\gamma)\leqslant 1,\qquad\sum_{\gamma\in\mathscr{P}}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|^{2}\lesssim 1. (2.34)

The first inequality is an equality when 𝒫\mathscr{P} is a finite cutset meeting every branch.

We first prove (2.26). Let Γℓ\Gamma_{\ell} be the family of first-stopping paths:

Γℓ:={γ:|ℳPF(γ−;z)|⩾2−ℓ,|ℳPF(γ;z)|<2−ℓ}.\Gamma_{\ell}:=\left\{\gamma:|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma^{-};z)|\geqslant 2^{-\ell},\quad|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|<2^{-\ell}\right\}.

Here γ−\gamma^{-} is the parent path. The one-step lower bounds imply

|ℳPF​(γ,z)|∼2−ℓ,μ⁡(γ)∼4−ℓ,γ∈Γℓ.|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma;z)|\sim 2^{-\ell},\qquad\mu(\gamma)\sim 4^{-\ell},\qquad\gamma\in\Gamma_{\ell}.

By Proposition 2.12, every branch reaches this stopping level within O⁡(1+ℓ)O(1+\ell) steps. Thus Γℓ\Gamma_{\ell} is a finite cutset. Since root paths are unique, its endpoints are in bijection with ∂ℬℓell\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}, and therefore

1=∑γ∈Γℓμ⁡(γ)∼4−ℓ​|Γℓ|=4−ℓ​|∂ℬℓell|.1=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma_{\ell}}\mu(\gamma)\sim 4^{-\ell}|\Gamma_{\ell}|=4^{-\ell}|\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}|.

This proves (2.26). We also obtain

|ℳPF(o↝y;z)|∼2−ℓ,y∈∂ℬℓell.|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(o\leadsto y;z)|\sim 2^{-\ell},\qquad y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}. (2.35)

We next prove the two-point estimate at the level of path weights. Fix i,j∈ℬℓelli,j\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}. For y∈∂ℬℓelly\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}, let b⁡(i,j,y)b(i,j,y) denote the common vertex of the three pairwise paths joining i,j,yi,j,y. For a fixed b∈i↝jb\in i\leadsto j, the paths from bb to boundary vertices satisfying b⁡(i,j,y)=bb(i,j,y)=b form a prefix-free family, since b∈i↝j⊂ℬℓellb\in i\leadsto j\subset{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}. Applying (2.34) with root bb gives

∑y∈∂ℬℓell:b⁡(i,j,y)=b|ℳPF(b↝y;z)|2≲1.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}:\\ b(i,j,y)=b\end{subarray}}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(b\leadsto y;z)|^{2}\lesssim 1.

By the multiplicative comparison,

∑y∈∂ℬℓell:b⁡(i,j,y)=b|ℳPF(i↝y;z)ℳPF(j↝y;z)|≲|ℳPF(i↝b;z)ℳPF(j↝b;z)|.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}:\\ b(i,j,y)=b\end{subarray}}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(i\leadsto y;z)\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto y;z)|\lesssim|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(i\leadsto b;z)\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto b;z)|. (2.36)

There are only O⁡(1)O(1) vertices of each dyadic elliptic level on i↝ji\leadsto j. Indeed, this path splits at anc⁡(i,j)\anc(i,j) into two root-directed segments, and the bound pe​f⩽1−cp_{ef}\leqslant 1-c gives geometric contraction along each segment away from oo, apart from the harmless first step. Summing (2.36) and using (2.32), we obtain

∑y∈∂ℬℓell|ℳPF(i↝y;z)ℳPF(j↝y;z)|≲∑b∈i↝j2−|ℓi−ℓb|−|ℓj−ℓb|≲∑t⩾02−|ℓi−t|−|ℓj−t|≲(1+|ℓi−ℓj|)2−|ℓi−ℓj|.\displaystyle\sum_{y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(i\leadsto y;z)\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto y;z)|\lesssim\sum_{b\in i\leadsto j}2^{-|\ell_{i}-\ell_{b}|-|\ell_{j}-\ell_{b}|}\lesssim\sum_{t\geqslant 0}2^{-|\ell_{i}-t|-|\ell_{j}-t|}\lesssim(1+|\ell_{i}-\ell_{j}|)2^{-|\ell_{i}-\ell_{j}|}. (2.37)

The last step separates the levels between ℓi\ell_{i} and ℓj\ell_{j} from the geometric tails. Together with (2.31), this proves (2.30).

Taking i=ji=j in (2.37) gives (2.27). Taking i=oi=o and using (2.35) gives

∑y∈∂ℬℓell|Gj​y|≲2ℓ∑y∈∂ℬℓell|ℳPF(o↝y;z)ℳPF(j↝y;z)|≲(1+ℓj)2ℓ−ℓj,\displaystyle\sum_{y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}}|G_{jy}|\lesssim 2^{\ell}\sum_{y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(o\leadsto y;z)\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto y;z)|\lesssim(1+\ell_{j})2^{\ell-\ell_{j}},

which proves (2.29).

Finally, Proposition 2.12 implies ℬℓell⊂ℬC⁡(1+ℓ)​(o,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}\subset{\mathcal{B}}_{C(1+\ell)}(o,{\mathcal{G}}). Increasing CC if necessary, every path from j∈ℬℓellj\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell} to another vertex of this subtree has length at most C⁡(1+ℓ)C(1+\ell). For each fixed length, the paths starting from jj form a prefix-free family. Hence (2.34) and Zj∼1Z_{j}\sim 1 give

∑y∈ℬℓell|Gj​y|2≲∑y∈ℬℓell|ℳPF(j↝y;z)|2≲∑k=0C⁡(1+ℓ)∑|γ|=k:γ​ starts at ​jμj(γ)≲1+ℓ≲ℓ.\displaystyle\sum_{y\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}}|G_{jy}|^{2}\lesssim\sum_{y\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto y;z)|^{2}\lesssim\sum_{k=0}^{C(1+\ell)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\gamma|=k:\\ \gamma\text{ starts at }j\end{subarray}}\mu_{j}(\gamma)\lesssim 1+\ell\lesssim\ell.

This proves (2.28).

The one-cycle case. Removing cycle-closing successors changes mass conservation into an inequality, but preserves (2.34). Thus the first-stopping family still satisfies |Γℓ|≲4ℓ|\Gamma_{\ell}|\lesssim 4^{\ell}. Consequently, |∂ℬℓell|≲4ℓ|\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}|\lesssim 4^{\ell}. The one-step lower bound also proves (2.35) for the actual boundary.

For the reverse cardinality bound, choose an edge out of oo whose forward component does not meet the cycle. Such an edge exists by the minimum-degree assumption. This branch carries a uniformly positive initial PF mass, and its vertices have unique simple paths from oo. The tree stopping argument therefore produces ≳4ℓ\gtrsim 4^{\ell} distinct genuine outer-boundary vertices. This proves (2.26).

To transfer the summation estimates, fix i,j∈ℬℓelli,j\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell} and let 𝒞\mathscr{C} consist of the unique cycle together with the tree paths connecting o,i,jo,i,j to it. Every component outside 𝒞\mathscr{C} is a tree attached to 𝒞\mathscr{C} at a unique vertex. For y∉𝒞y\notin\mathscr{C}, let b⁡(y)b(y) denote this attachment point, and set b⁡(y)=yb(y)=y for y∈𝒞y\in\mathscr{C}. For a fixed attachment point bb, every path from o,i,jo,i,j to a vertex yy with b⁡(y)=bb(y)=b has the same terminal tree segment b↝yb\leadsto y. Hence, by the multiplicative comparison of the PF weights,

|ℳPF(i↝y;z)ℳPF(j↝y;z)|≲|ℳPF(i↝b;z)ℳPF(j↝b;z)||ℳPF(b↝y;z)|2.|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(i\leadsto y;z)\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto y;z)|\lesssim|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(i\leadsto b;z)\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto b;z)||\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(b\leadsto y;z)|^{2}.

Moreover, the elliptic neighborhood intersects each attached tree in an initial subtree. Therefore the paths from bb to its outer boundary form a prefix-free family, and the tree estimate gives

∑y∈∂ℬℓell:b⁡(y)=b|ℳPF(b↝y;z)|2≲1.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}:\\ b(y)=b\end{subarray}}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(b\leadsto y;z)|^{2}\lesssim 1.\vskip-8.53581pt

Thus the fixed-bb estimate

∑y∈∂ℬℓell:b⁡(y)=b|ℳPF(i↝y;z)ℳPF(j↝y;z)|≲|ℳPF(i↝b;z)ℳPF(j↝b;z)|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}:\\ b(y)=b\end{subarray}}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(i\leadsto y;z)\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto y;z)|\lesssim|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(i\leadsto b;z)\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto b;z)|\vskip-5.69054pt

is exactly the same as in the tree case. The corresponding interior estimate follows from the same length-layer argument.

It remains only to sum over the possible attachment points. We claim that there are O⁡(1)\OO(1) vertices of 𝒞\mathscr{C} in each dyadic PF level. Indeed, the tree part of 𝒞\mathscr{C} consists of a bounded number of paths along which the PF weights vary geometrically. On the cycle, there are two simple paths from the attachment point of oo to a given vertex, and

|ℳPF(o↝b;z)|∼max{|ℳPF(γ+(b);z)|,|ℳPF(γ−(b);z)|},|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(o\leadsto b;z)|\sim\max\{|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma_{+}(b);z)|,\,|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(\gamma_{-}(b);z)|\},

where γ+​(b)\gamma_{+}(b) and γ−​(b)\gamma_{-}(b) denote the two simple paths from oo to bb, obtained by following the two different directions around the cycle. As bb moves around the cycle, the two directional path weights vary geometrically in opposite directions, since each additional step multiplies the squared PF weight by pe​fp_{ef} with c⩽pe​f⩽1−cc\leqslant p_{ef}\leqslant 1-c. Hence, for every tt,

#{b∈𝒞:|ℳPF(o↝b;z)|∼2−t}≲1.\#\left\{b\in\mathscr{C}:|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(o\leadsto b;z)|\sim 2^{-t}\right\}\lesssim 1.

Therefore the summation over bb reduces to exactly the same dyadic-level summation as in the tree case.

Using (2.32), we may therefore repeat the summation in (2.37), with b∈𝒞b\in\mathscr{C} in place of b∈i↝jb\in i\leadsto j. This proves the same two-point path-weight bound, from which (2.30), (2.27), and (2.29) follow exactly as above. For the interior bound, each relevant terminal tree segment has length O⁡(ℓ)O(\ell), since it belongs to a root path of weight at least 2−ℓ2^{-\ell}. The same length-layer estimate consequently gives

∑y∈ℬℓell|Gj​y|2≲ℓ∑b∈𝒞|ℳPF(j↝b;z)|2≲ℓ∑t⩾04−|ℓj−t|≲ℓ.\displaystyle\sum_{y\in{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}}|G_{jy}|^{2}\lesssim\ell\sum_{b\in\mathscr{C}}|\mathcal{M}^{\rm PF}(j\leadsto b;z)|^{2}\lesssim\ell\sum_{t\geqslant 0}4^{-|\ell_{j}-t|}\lesssim\ell.

This proves (2.28) and completes the proof. ∎

2.3 Extension with weights

Definition 2.19 (Extension with weight q⁡(z)q(z)).

Let q⁡(z)=(qe​(z))e∈E→ℋq(z)=\bigl(q_{e}(z)\bigr)_{e\in\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{H}}}} be a collection of weights indexed by the directed edge types of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}. The extension of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} with weight q⁡(z)q(z), denoted by Ext⁡(𝒢,q⁡(z)),\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{G}},q(z)), is obtained by assigning every vertex v∈𝔾v\in{\mathbb{G}} the weight −∑e∈ℳ𝒢​(v)qe(z)-\sum_{e\in\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{G}}(v)}q_{e}(z) . We regard Ext⁡(𝒢,q⁡(z))\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{G}},q(z)) as a virtual graph and write G⁡(Ext⁡(𝒢,q⁡(z)),z)G(\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{G}},q(z)),z) for its Green’s function.

Equivalently, if AA denotes the adjacency matrix of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}, then the matrix associated with the extension is

A−∑v∈𝔾∑e∈ℳ𝒢​(v)qe​(z)​ev​v,A-\sum_{v\in{\mathbb{G}}}\sum_{e\in\mathscr{M}_{\mathcal{G}}(v)}q_{e}(z)e_{vv},

where (ev​v)i​j=δv​i​δv​j.(e_{vv})_{ij}=\delta_{vi}\delta_{vj}. Hence its Green’s function is

The above extension with weight can be viewed as a general tree extension. The localization principle shows that, up to a controlled error, the Green function Gi​jG_{ij} depends only on a local neighborhood of ii and jj, so that the ambient graph 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} may be replaced by any subgraph 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} containing ℬr​(i,j,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(i,j,{\mathcal{G}}). In particular, it allows us to enlarge ℬr​(i,j,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(i,j,{\mathcal{G}}) by including additional vertices that are relevant to the argument and then work on the resulting localized subgraph; this procedure will be used repeatedly in Section 5.

Lemma 2.23 (Localization principle).

Fix z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with |z|⩽2​dmax|z|\leqslant 2d_{\rm max}. Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be a finite connected subgraph of a lift of ℋ{\mathcal{H}}, containing at most one cycle. |Gi​j​(Ext⁡(𝒢,q),z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(𝒦,q),z)|≲(1+diam⁡(𝒢))​|R⁡(q,z)|∞+β2​r.\left|G_{ij}(\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{G}},q),z)-G_{ij}(\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{K}},q),z)\right|\lesssim(1+\diam({\mathcal{G}}))|R(q,z)|_{\infty}+\beta^{2r}.
Remark 2.24.

The localization principle also applies to the mixed extensions arising in the switching arguments in Section 5 and Section 6. Exact universal-cover branches attached to the retained subgraph 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} are kept intact, while those attached outside 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} are separated from the vertices under consideration. By the resolvent identity and the β\beta-decay of the corresponding Green functions, their total contribution is absorbed into the existing localization error. The same convention is preserved before and after switching, with exact branches reattached intact.

Since the proofs of all the above lemmas consist of direct computations and closely follow the corresponding arguments in [42, Section 2.3], we defer them to Appendix B.

3 Local Resampling and Geometric Control

In this section, we introduce a local resampling procedure adapted to the elliptic neighborhood introduced in Definition 2.16. The construction is the random-lift analogue of the local resampling for random dd-regular graphs in [42], with the metric neighborhood replaced by the elliptic neighborhood and with all switchings required to preserve the oriented edge types of the base graph.

3.1 Elliptic Local Resampling

Definition 3.1 (Type-preserving switching).

Let e1=(v1,v2)e_{1}=(v_{1},v_{2}) and e2=(v3,v4)e_{2}=(v_{3},v_{4}) be two disjoint oriented lift edges with the same type. The switching encoded by S→={e1,e2}\vec{S}=\{e_{1},e_{2}\} replaces the unoriented edges {v1,v2}\{v_{1},v_{2}\} and {v3,v4}\{v_{3},v_{4}\} by {v1,v4}\{v_{1},v_{4}\} and {v3,v2}\{v_{3},v_{2}\}. Since the two original edges have the same oriented base-edge type, the two new edges have the same type as well. Thus the switching preserves the covering map and TS→​(𝒢)∈𝖦N​(ℋ)T_{\vec{S}}({\mathcal{G}})\in{\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}).

Following our previous convention, we denote its vertex set by 𝕋\mathbb{T} and define its oriented edge boundary set by ∂E→𝒯:={(x,y)∈E→𝒢:x∈𝕋,y∉𝕋}.\partial_{\vec{E}}{\mathcal{T}}:=\left\{(x,y)\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{G}}:x\in\mathbb{T},\ y\notin\mathbb{T}\right\}. We then enumerate ∂E→𝒯={e1,…,eμ},\partial_{\vec{E}}{\mathcal{T}}=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{\mu}\}, where eα=(lα,aα)e_{\alpha}=(l_{\alpha},a_{\alpha}) with lα∈𝕋l_{\alpha}\in\mathbb{T} and aα∉𝕋.a_{\alpha}\notin\mathbb{T}. S→α:={(lα,aα),(bα,cα)},𝐒:=(S→1,…,S→μ).\vec{S}_{\alpha}:=\left\{(l_{\alpha},a_{\alpha}),(b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha})\right\},\qquad{\bf S}:=(\vec{S}_{1},\dots,\vec{S}_{\mu}). (3.1)

The collection 𝐒{\bf S} will be called the resampling data for 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}.

For α∈⟦1,μ⟧\alpha\in\llbracket 1,\mu\rrbracket, define the indicator function Iα​(𝒢,𝐒)=1I_{\alpha}({\mathcal{G}},{\bf S})=1 if the local neighborhood ℬℜ/4​({aα,bα,cα},𝒢(𝕋)){\mathcal{B}}_{{\mathfrak{R}}/4}(\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\},{\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}) after adding the edge {aα,bα}\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha}\} is a tree. Otherwise we set Iα=0I_{\alpha}=0. We further define Jα​(𝒢,𝐒)=1J_{\alpha}({\mathcal{G}},{\bf S})=1 if dist𝒢(𝕋)​({aα,bα,cα},{aβ,bβ,cβ})>ℜ/4\mathrm{dist}_{{\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}}\left(\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\},\{a_{\beta},b_{\beta},c_{\beta}\}\right)>{\mathfrak{R}}/4 for every β∈⟦1,μ⟧∖{α},\beta\in\llbracket 1,\mu\rrbracket\setminus\{\alpha\}, and Jα=0J_{\alpha}=0 otherwise.

The two indicator functions encode two different geometric requirements. First, the condition Iα=1I_{\alpha}=1 imposes both a local tree condition and a separation condition. Indeed, it implies that ℬℜ/4​(aα,𝒢(𝕋)){\mathcal{B}}_{{\mathfrak{R}}/4}(a_{\alpha},{\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}) and ℬℜ/4​({bα,cα},𝒢(𝕋)){\mathcal{B}}_{{\mathfrak{R}}/4}(\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\},{\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}) are both trees. Together with the edge {bα,cα}\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\}, adding the new edge {aα,bα}\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha}\} would then create a cycle, contradicting Iα=1I_{\alpha}=1.

On the other hand, JαJ_{\alpha} is an isolation condition between different switching pairs. If Jα=1J_{\alpha}=1, then for every β≠α\beta\neq\alpha, the support {aβ,bβ,cβ}\{a_{\beta},b_{\beta},c_{\beta}\} of the β\beta-th switching lies outside the radius-ℜ/4{\mathfrak{R}}/4 neighborhood used to define IαI_{\alpha}. This separation prevents interactions between distinct simple switchings and, in particular, guarantees that the admissibility condition is stable under the local resampling. See Figure 4 for details.
