We record the basic structural properties of the local resampling map. The proposition below shows that the switching preserves the geometry relevant to the elliptic neighborhood and the separation of the switching cells, while also preserving the admissible graph class. Moreover, the reverse switching is well defined and the corresponding transformations preserve the underlying sampling measures. These facts will be used repeatedly when transferring estimates between the original and resampled graphs.

Proposition 3.3.

For any switching data 𝐒∈𝖲⁡(𝒢){\bf S}\in{\sf S}({\mathcal{G}}), we have

  1. (i)

    The elliptic neighborhood is invariant under the local resampling: ℬℓell​(o,T𝐒​(𝒢),z)=ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z).{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,T_{\bf S}({\mathcal{G}});z)={\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z).

  2. (ii)

    The radius-ℜ/8{\mathfrak{R}}/8 neighborhoods of the root before and after the switching are isomorphic as rooted graphs:

    ℬℜ/8​(o,𝒢)≃ℬℜ/8​(o,T𝐒​(𝒢)).{\mathcal{B}}_{{\mathfrak{R}}/8}(o,{\mathcal{G}})\simeq{\mathcal{B}}_{{\mathfrak{R}}/8}(o,T_{\bf S}({\mathcal{G}})).
  3. (iii)

    For every α∈𝖶𝐒\alpha\in\mathsf{W}_{\bf S}, the switching cell {aα,bα,cα}\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\} remains separated from all the other switching cells by distance larger than ℜ/4{\mathfrak{R}}/4 both before and after the switching:

    dist𝒢(𝕋)​({aα,bα,cα},⋃β≠α{aβ,bβ,cβ})>ℜ4,distT𝐒​(𝒢)(𝕋)​({aα,bα,cα},⋃β≠α{aβ,bβ,cβ})>ℜ4.\mathrm{dist}_{{\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}}\big(\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\},\bigcup_{\beta\neq\alpha}\{a_{\beta},b_{\beta},c_{\beta}\}\big)>\frac{{\mathfrak{R}}}{4},\quad\mathrm{dist}_{T_{\bf S}({\mathcal{G}})^{(\mathbb{T})}}\big(\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\},\bigcup_{\beta\neq\alpha}\{a_{\beta},b_{\beta},c_{\beta}\}\big)>\frac{{\mathfrak{R}}}{4}.
  4. (iv)

    For every 𝒢∈𝖦N​(ℋ){\mathcal{G}}\in{\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}), T~\widetilde{T} is an involution: T~∘T~=i​d\widetilde{T}\circ\widetilde{T}=\mspace{2mu}\mathrm{i}\mspace{-0.6mu}\mathrm{d}.

  5. (v)

    The maps T~\widetilde{T} and TT are measure preserving : ℙ′∘T~−1=ℙ′\mathbb{P}^{\prime}\circ\widetilde{T}^{-1}=\mathbb{P}^{\prime} and ℙ′∘T−1=ℙ\mathbb{P}^{\prime}\circ T^{-1}=\mathbb{P}.

Proof.

Write 𝒢~=T𝐒​(𝒢)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}=T_{\bf S}({\mathcal{G}}) and ℂα={aα,bα,cα}{\mathbb{C}}_{\alpha}=\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\}. The invariance property follows directly from Remark 2.17.

For the second assertion, each admissible switching replaces the branch attached through {lα,aα}\{l_{\alpha},a_{\alpha}\} by the branch attached through {lα,cα}\{l_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\}. The condition Iα=1I_{\alpha}=1 ensures that both branches are trees on the relevant scale. Since the switching preserves edge types, these branches have the same rooted type-labelled structure. Moreover, the separation condition Jα=1J_{\alpha}=1, which places distinct switching cells at distance larger than ℜ/4{\mathfrak{R}}/4, guarantees that their portions visible inside the radius-ℜ/8{\mathfrak{R}}/8 neighborhood of oo cannot meet: otherwise two such portions would connect the corresponding switching cells by a path of length at most 2​(ℜ/8)=ℜ/42({\mathfrak{R}}/8)={\mathfrak{R}}/4. Replacing these branches by their type-preserving counterparts therefore gives a rooted isomorphism ℬℜ/8​(o,𝒢)≃ℬℜ/8​(o,𝒢~),{\mathcal{B}}_{{\mathfrak{R}}/8}(o,{\mathcal{G}})\simeq{\mathcal{B}}_{{\mathfrak{R}}/8}(o,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}), which fixes 𝒯{\mathcal{T}}.

The separation in the original graph follows from Jα=1J_{\alpha}=1. In the exterior graph, every modified edge has both endpoints in a single switching cell. If a path of length at most ℜ/4{\mathfrak{R}}/4 in 𝒢~(𝕋)\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})} connected ℂα{\mathbb{C}}_{\alpha} to another cell, the segment between its last departure from ℂα{\mathbb{C}}_{\alpha} and its first visit to another cell would contain only unchanged edges. This would contradict the original separation, proving the third assertion. For the involution and measure-preserving properties, the arguments in [42, Proposition 3.3 and Proposition 3.5] apply without essential modification. Indeed, the admissibility conditions are preserved by reversal, and the numbers of available exterior edges of each type are determined by the fixed type-labelled neighborhood 𝒯{\mathcal{T}}. ∎

Remark 3.4.

The local resampling constructed above is defined for a fixed zz, since the elliptic neighborhood ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z){\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}^{\rm ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z) depends on zz. Thus, more precisely, the maps above should be regarded as T~z\widetilde{T}_{z} and Tz.T_{z}. However, for simplicity, we suppress the dependence on z, since it plays no essential role in the proof.

In Section 4, our argument requires two successive local resampling procedures. For the first resampling, the definition of Ω¯\bar{\Omega} in Definition 1.1 provides the required control of the local geometry of the original graph 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}. The second resampling, however, is performed on the already resampled graph T𝐒​𝒢T_{\mathbf{S}}{\mathcal{G}}. It is therefore necessary to understand how the geometric properties encoded in Ω¯\bar{\Omega} are affected by one local resampling. In the rest of this subsection, we show that, although some of these properties may deteriorate slightly after resampling, the resulting graph still retains sufficiently good local geometry for the second resampling step. To formulate the weaker geometric conditions that will be used for the resampled graphs, we introduce the following definition.

Definition 3.5.

Given a base graph ℋ{\mathcal{H}} and a large constant 𝔮{\mathfrak{q}}, let Ω¯+⊂𝖦N​(ℋ)\bar{\Omega}^{+}\subset{\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}) denote the set of graphs:

  • •

    The radius-ℜ/8{\mathfrak{R}}/8 neighborhood of every vertex contains at most one cycle.

  • •

    The radius-ℜ/2{\mathfrak{R}}/2 neighborhood of every vertex has excess at most C​𝔮C{\mathfrak{q}}, where CC is a universal constant.

  • •

    The number of vertices that have a radius-ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} neighborhood that contains a cycle is at most 2​N𝔠2N^{{\mathfrak{c}}}.

Notice that the sets Ω¯\bar{\Omega} defined in Definition 1.1 and Ω¯+\bar{\Omega}^{+} are subsets of 𝖦N​(ℋ){\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}) defined by deterministic properties. It is clear that Ω¯⊂Ω¯+\bar{\Omega}\subset\bar{\Omega}^{+}. Compared with Ω¯\bar{\Omega}, the set Ω¯+\bar{\Omega}^{+} should be viewed as a relaxed version of the good geometric set. Moreover, for any graph in Ω¯+\bar{\Omega}^{+}, the radius-ℜ/8{\mathfrak{R}}/8 neighborhood of every vertex contains at most one cycle. Therefore, Proposition 2.15 applies to the tree extension of the radius-ℜ/8{\mathfrak{R}}/8 neighborhood of every vertex in such a graph.

Remark.

The second condition in Definition 3.5 serves a different purpose from the first one. If a neighborhood has excess larger than one, the tree-extension estimates established above are in general no longer available for controlling the corresponding Green function. Thus, the radius-ℜ/2{\mathfrak{R}}/2 excess bound is not imposed in order to obtain Green function estimates on that scale. Rather, this condition will be used in the geometric counting arguments below. In addition to the Green function estimates on radius-ℜ/8{\mathfrak{R}}/8 neighborhoods, we shall need to control the number of atypical vertices whose radius-ℜ/2{\mathfrak{R}}/2 neighborhoods fail to have the desired tree-like structure. The uniform bound on the excess of radius-ℜ/2{\mathfrak{R}}/2 neighborhoods provides the geometric input needed for this counting argument.

The next proposition shows that a typical local resampling of a graph 𝒢∈Ω¯{\mathcal{G}}\in\bar{\Omega} belongs to Ω¯+\bar{\Omega}^{+}. The proof is purely geometric and is the same as [42, Proposition 5.12]; we therefore omit it.

Proposition 3.6.

For every large constant 𝔮{\mathfrak{q}} and every graph 𝒢∈Ω¯{\mathcal{G}}\in\bar{\Omega}, there exists a event F0​(𝒢)⊂𝖲​(𝒢)F_{0}({\mathcal{G}})\subset{\sf S}({\mathcal{G}}) with probability ℙ𝒢​(F0​(𝒢))=1−O⁡(N−𝔮)\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G}}(F_{0}({\mathcal{G}}))=1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}) such that, for every switching data 𝐒∈F0​(𝒢)\mathbf{S}\in F_{0}({\mathcal{G}}), T𝖲​(𝒢)∈Ω¯+T_{\mathsf{S}}({\mathcal{G}})\in\bar{\Omega}^{+}.

We first analyze the geometric properties of the boundary vertices {aα}α=1μ\{a_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha=1}^{\mu}. This part is deterministic, since aαa_{\alpha} is fixed once 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} and 𝕋\mathbb{T} are fixed; the randomness of the local sampling enters only through the subsequently sampled vertices bαb_{\alpha} and cαc_{\alpha}.

Lemma 3.7 (Proposition 5.2 of [42]).

Let 𝒢∈𝖦N​(ℋ){\mathcal{G}}\in{\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}) and recall that 𝒯=ℬℓell​(o,𝒢){\mathcal{T}}={\mathcal{B}}^{\rm ell}_{\ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}}) is the elliptic neighborhood defined in Definition 2.16. α,β∈𝖢s for some s⟺aα and aβ belong to the same connected component of 𝒜.\alpha,\beta\in{\sf C}_{s}\text{ for some }s\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_{\alpha}\text{ and }a_{\beta}\text{ belong to the same connected component of }{\mathcal{A}}.

∑s=1n𝟏{|𝖢s|⩾2}|𝖢s|⩽2ω.\sum_{s=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}_{\{|{\sf C}_{s}|\geqslant 2\}}\,|{\sf C}_{s}|\leqslant 2\omega. (3.10)

Proposition 3.9 (Tree neighborhoods of the boundary vertices).

Under the same assumptions as in Lemma 3.7, we have

|{α∈[[1,μ]]:ℬR/2​(aα,𝒢(𝕋))​ is not a tree}|⩽3​ω.\left|\left\{\alpha\in[\![{1,\mu}]\!]:{\mathcal{B}}_{R/2}(a_{\alpha},\mathcal{G}^{(\mathbb{T})})\text{ is not a tree}\right\}\right|\leqslant 3\omega.

We next turn to the geometric properties involving {bα,cα}α=1μ\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha=1}^{\mu}. Unlike the boundary vertices aαa_{\alpha}, these vertices are chosen randomly by the local sampling. We therefore begin with the following elementary approximate-uniformity estimate, which will be used repeatedly to control the probability of geometric coincidences.

Lemma 3.10.

Given 𝒢∈𝖦N​(ℋ){\mathcal{G}}\in{\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}), for any vertex x∈𝔾∖𝕋x\in{\mathbb{G}}\setminus\mathbb{T} and α∈[[1,μ]]\alpha\in[\![{1,\mu}]\!]

ℙ𝒢​(bα=x)≲N−1,ℙ𝒢​(cα=x)≲N−1.\mathbb{P}_{{\mathcal{G}}}(b_{\alpha}=x)\lesssim N^{-1},\qquad\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G}}(c_{\alpha}=x)\lesssim N^{-1}. (3.11)

We recall that, for any α∈⟦1,μ⟧\alpha\in\llbracket 1,\mu\rrbracket, the oriented edge (bα,cα)(b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}) is chosen uniformly from the set E→𝒢(𝕋)eα\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}}^{\,e_{\alpha}}. Hence, we have |E→𝒢(𝕋)eα|≳N\bigl|\vec{E}_{{\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}}^{\,e_{\alpha}}\bigr|\gtrsim N, which directly gives (3.11). ∎

We next introduce the basic good event on which the local resampling will be performed. Since the edges {bα,cα}\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\} are chosen randomly in 𝒢(𝕋){\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}, the required separation and tree-neighborhood conditions are not deterministic. The following proposition shows that, after excluding an event of probability O⁡(N−𝔮)\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}), these geometric conditions fail for only O⁡(𝔮)\OO({\mathfrak{q}}) indices. In particular, on this good event, all but a bounded number of indices are admissible for the local sampling. This event will serve as the geometric foundation for the subsequent local resampling argument. The proof of Proposition 3.11 is almost identical to that of [42, Proposition 5.10 and Proposition 5.11], and we therefore omit the details.

Proposition 3.11.

For any large 𝔮∈ℕ+{\mathfrak{q}}\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and a graph 𝒢∈Ω¯{\mathcal{G}}\in\bar{\Omega} or Ω¯+\bar{\Omega}^{+}, there exists an event F1​(𝒢)⊂𝖲​(𝒢)F_{1}({\mathcal{G}})\subset\mathsf{S}({\mathcal{G}}) with probability ℙ𝒢​(F1​(𝒢))=1−O⁡(N−𝔮)\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G}}(F_{1}({\mathcal{G}}))=1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}) such that the following estimates hold:

  • •

    Most indices α∈[[1,μ]]\alpha\in[\![{1,\mu}]\!] are good in the following sense:

    |𝖡1|≲𝔮,with ​𝖡1={α∈[[1,μ]]:dist𝒢(𝕋)​(aα,{bα,cα})⩽ℜ/2+2},\displaystyle|{\mathsf{B}}_{1}|\lesssim{\mathfrak{q}},\text{with }{\mathsf{B}}_{1}=\{\alpha\in[\![{1,\mu}]\!]:{\mathrm{dist}_{\mathcal{G}^{(\mathbb{T})}}(a_{\alpha},\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\})\leqslant{\mathfrak{R}}/2+2}\}, (3.13)

4 Quantitative Local Law and Proof Strategy

In this section, we formulate the quantitative local law that will be proved in the remainder of the paper and describe the main structure of its proof. We first collect the parameters and error scales used throughout the argument.

4.1 Choice of parameters

Definition 4.1.

Fix parameters δ,β,𝔠∈(0,1),𝔞>6,𝔟⩾16​𝔞\delta,\beta,{\mathfrak{c}}\in(0,1),{\mathfrak{a}}>6,{\mathfrak{b}}\geqslant 16{\mathfrak{a}} and a large constant 𝔮{\mathfrak{q}}. After enlarging β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) if necessary, assume that N−1+c⩽β2​rN^{-1+c}\leqslant\beta^{2r}. The radius parameters are defined by: ℜ=(𝔠/4)​log⁡N,r=(𝔠/200)​log⁡N{\mathfrak{R}}=({\mathfrak{c}}/4)\log N,r=({\mathfrak{c}}/200)\log N and ℓ=𝔞​log4​log⁡N\ell={\mathfrak{a}}\log_{4}\log N. We denote by μ=|∂ℬℓell|\mu=\bigl|\partial{\mathcal{B}}^{\rm ell}_{\ell}\bigr| the cardinality of the boundary of the elliptic ball of radius ℓ\ell. We restrict to the spectral domain z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with η=Im⁡[z]⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N\eta=\im[z]\geqslant(\log N)^{{\mathfrak{b}}}/N. ℜ/50⩾r=O⁡(log⁡N)≫ℓ=O⁡(log4⁡log⁡N),μ∼4ℓ∼(log⁡N)𝔞,{\mathfrak{R}}/50\geqslant r=\OO(\log N)\gg\ell=\OO(\log_{4}\log N),\qquad\mu\sim 4^{\ell}\sim(\log N)^{{\mathfrak{a}}}, (4.1)

where μ∼4ℓ\mu\sim 4^{\ell} follows from (2.26). Define the baseline error by

ε⁡(z):=46​ℓ​(βr+|Im⁡mver​(z)|∞N​η+εedge+εcusp),\varepsilon(z):=4^{6\ell}\left(\beta^{r}+\sqrt{\frac{|\im m^{\rm ver}(z)|_{\infty}}{N\eta}}+\varepsilon_{\rm edge}+\varepsilon_{\rm cusp}\right), (4.2)

where |Im​mver|∞|{\mathrm{Im}}m^{\rm ver}|_{\infty} satisfies the bound from Lemma 2.6 and

εedge(z):=maxτ∈𝒮edge1Nη(|z−τ|+(Nη)−2/3)1/2,εcusp(z):=maxτ∈𝒮cusp1Nη(|z−τ|+(Nη)−3/5)2/3.\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\rm edge}(z):=\max_{\tau\in\mathcal{S}_{\rm edge}}\frac{1}{N\eta\bigl(|z-\tau|+(N\eta)^{-2/3}\bigr)^{1/2}},\qquad\varepsilon_{\rm cusp}(z):=\max_{\tau\in\mathcal{S}_{\rm cusp}}\frac{1}{N\eta\bigl(|z-\tau|+(N\eta)^{-3/5}\bigr)^{2/3}}. (4.3)

The maximum over an empty set is understood to be zero. Let ε∗​(z)\varepsilon_{*}(z) be the stability error scale defined in (4.5). Finally, define

φ⁡(z):=4ℓ​|Im⁡mver​(z)|∞+ε∗​(z)+(log⁡N)​ε​(z)N​η,\varphi(z):=4^{\ell}\sqrt{\frac{|\im m^{\rm ver}(z)|_{\infty}+\varepsilon_{*}(z)+(\log N)\varepsilon(z)}{N\eta}}, (4.4)

where

ε∗​(z):={ε⁡(z)(ε⁡(z)+|z−τ|)1/2,if z lies near a regular edge τ,ε⁡(z)(ε⁡(z)+|z−τ|)2/3,if z lies near a regular cusp τ,ε⁡(z),otherwise.\varepsilon_{*}(z):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\varepsilon(z)}{\bigl(\varepsilon(z)+|z-\tau|\bigr)^{1/2}},&\text{if $z$ lies near a regular edge $\tau$},\\[8.53581pt] \displaystyle\frac{\varepsilon(z)}{\bigl(\varepsilon(z)+|z-\tau|\bigr)^{2/3}},&\text{if $z$ lies near a regular cusp $\tau$},\\[8.53581pt] \varepsilon(z),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (4.5)

With these choices, uniformly on the spectral domain under consideration,

ε⁡(z)≲4−2​ℓ,φ⁡(z)≲(log⁡N)1/2​4−2​ℓ​ε​(z).\varepsilon(z)\lesssim 4^{-2\ell},\qquad\varphi(z)\lesssim(\log N)^{1/2}4^{-2\ell}\varepsilon(z). (4.6)

These estimates provide all the error absorptions needed in the remaining proof.

We next explain the roles and choices of the above parameters. The parameter δ>0\delta>0 is the regularity parameter introduced in Lemma 2.2, which keeps the spectral domain away from the singular set while retaining the regular edges and cusps under consideration. The constant β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) is the path-decay rate from Proposition 2.12, and determines the localization error βr\beta^{r}.

The three radii ℜ{\mathfrak{R}}, rr, and ℓ\ell serve different purposes. The radius ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} controls the local tree-like geometry. For graphs in either Ω¯\bar{\Omega} or Ω¯+\bar{\Omega}^{+}, every radius-ℜ/8{\mathfrak{R}}/8 neighborhood contains at most one cycle. This is the geometric condition needed for the deterministic Green-function estimates in Lemma 2.20 and the localization principle in Lemma 2.23. In particular, the localized Green function can be controlled through the corresponding tree-extension model, with the possible cycle retained in the finite core. The radius rr determines the size of the neighborhood used in this localization. We choose r⩽ℜ/50r\leqslant{\mathfrak{R}}/50 to leave room for the local enlargements appearing below: each relevant connected component of the unions of rr-neighborhoods must remain inside a radius-ℜ/8{\mathfrak{R}}/8 neighborhood.

The elliptic radius ℓ\ell determines the size of the resampling boundary. We have μ∼4ℓ∼(log⁡N)𝔞\mu\sim 4^{\ell}\sim(\log N)^{\mathfrak{a}} The boundary averaging in Proposition 6.1 produces a gain of order 2−ℓ2^{-\ell}. Hence ℓ\ell must be large enough so that this gain dominates the logarithmic losses appearing in the concentration and reconstruction estimates. This is the reason for choosing 𝔞>6{\mathfrak{a}}>6. On the other hand, the resampling boundary should not grow too fast. Indeed, the switching argument samples vertices attached to the boundary, and its error estimates involve unions and sums over boundary indices. Keeping 4ℓ=(log⁡N)𝔞4^{\ell}=(\log N)^{\mathfrak{a}} polylogarithmic ensures that collisions among the sampled vertices, intersections with exceptional local neighborhoods, and the losses from summing over the boundary remain negligible.

The parameter ε∗\varepsilon_{*} is the stability-adjusted error scale. Indeed, the bootstrap first yields |R⁡(Q,z)|∞≲ε⁡(z),|R(Q,z)|_{\infty}\lesssim\varepsilon(z), and Lemma 2.7 then gives |Q−m⁡(z)|∞≲ε∗​(z).|Q-m(z)|_{\infty}\lesssim\varepsilon_{*}(z). In the stable bulk there is no stability loss, so ε∗∼ε\varepsilon_{*}\sim\varepsilon. Near a regular edge or cusp, however, the Dyson equation becomes degenerate, and the resulting error may deteriorate to ε1/2\varepsilon^{1/2} and ε1/3\varepsilon^{1/3} respectively. Therefore, close to an edge or cusp, ε∗\varepsilon_{*} can be much larger than the baseline error ε\varepsilon.

We next explain the two error parameters φ\varphi and ε\varepsilon. The quantity φ\varphi is not an independent error scale. It is chosen directly from the Ward-identity estimate (5.32) so that, for each fixed vertex, only an O⁡(4−2​ℓ)\OO(4^{-2\ell}) proportion of the other vertices can have Green-function entries larger than φ\varphi. See section 5.3 for details.

The main quantity that has to be chosen is ε\varepsilon. Its first contribution, βr\beta^{r}, is the deterministic localization error coming from replacing a Green function by the corresponding radius-rr local model. See Proposition 4.5 for details.

The term |Im​mver​(z)|∞/(N​η)\sqrt{|{\mathrm{Im}}m^{\rm ver}(z)|_{\infty}/(N\eta)} is the natural fluctuation scale coming from the Ward identity. However, the diagonal Green function is not approximated by mverm^{\rm ver} with error ε\varepsilon itself, but rather with the stability error ε∗\varepsilon_{*}. Near a regular edge or cusp, ε∗\varepsilon_{*} is larger because the Dyson equation becomes less stable. Substituting this weaker control back into the Ward estimate produces the additional errors εedge\varepsilon_{\rm edge} and εcusp\varepsilon_{\rm cusp}. Their definitions are chosen so that they reproduce the natural self-consistent scales (Nη)−2/3(N\eta)^{-2/3} near a regular edge and (Nη)−3/5(N\eta)^{-3/5} near a regular cusp, while retaining the stronger bounds (N​η)−1(N\eta)^{-1} away from the corresponding regular edge or cusp.

Finally, the prefactor 46​ℓ4^{6\ell} in (4.2) is a bookkeeping buffer for the switching argument. Several estimates below involve sums over one or two boundary indices, and therefore lose powers of 4ℓ4^{\ell}. Enlarging the basic error by 46​ℓ4^{6\ell} ensures that, after passing through the Ward estimate and the boundary summations, the resulting quantity φ\varphi is still much smaller than ε\varepsilon.

An important feature of the error parameter ε\varepsilon is its monotonicity along vertical lines. For fixed EE, the error ε⁡(E+i​η)\varepsilon(E+\mathrm{i}\eta) is non-increasing in η\eta. Indeed, the Ward term has this property by the Stieltjes transform representation, and the edge and cusp correction terms in (4.3) are also non-increasing in η\eta. Hence, for t⩾ηt\geqslant\eta, ε⁡(E+i​t)⩽ε⁡(E+i​η).\varepsilon(E+\mathrm{i}t)\leqslant\varepsilon(E+\mathrm{i}\eta). Therefore the residual along the whole vertical continuation segment can be controlled by the single endpoint error ε⁡(E+i​η)\varepsilon(E+\mathrm{i}\eta), as required in the edge and cusp stability Lemma 2.7.

The lower bound N​η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟N\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{\mathfrak{b}} has the following role: it guarantees that the Ward fluctuations and the edge/cusp corrections remain sufficiently small even after the factor 46​ℓ4^{6\ell} is inserted. Since 4ℓ∼(log⁡N)𝔞4^{\ell}\sim(\log N)^{\mathfrak{a}}, the condition 𝔟⩾16​𝔞{\mathfrak{b}}\geqslant 16{\mathfrak{a}} leaves enough room for all the required polylogarithmic losses.

4.2 Quantitative Local Law and Continuation Argument

We first state the quantitative local law, which holds throughout the regular spectral regime away from the singular energies, including the stable bulk, regular edges, and regular cusps.

Theorem 4.2.

Fix any sufficiently large 𝔮∈ℕ+{\mathfrak{q}}\in\mathbb{N}_{+} and let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be sampled uniformly from Ω¯\bar{\Omega} defined in Definition 1.1. For every sufficiently large N∈ℕ+N\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, with probability 1−O⁡(N−𝔮)1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}), the Green’s function of 𝒢∈Ω¯{\mathcal{G}}\in\bar{\Omega} satisfies, uniformly for z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with η=Im⁡[z]⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N\eta=\im[z]\geqslant(\log N)^{\mathfrak{b}}/N,

|Gi​j​(𝒢,z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢),m⁡(z)),z)|≲ε∗​(z),\big|G_{ij}({\mathcal{G}},z)-G_{ij}(\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}),m(z)),z)\big|\lesssim\varepsilon_{*}(z), (4.7)

and the vector of type-averaged diagonal Green functions satisfies

|Qver​(z)−mver​(z)|∞≲ε∗​(z),|Q^{\rm ver}(z)-m^{\rm ver}(z)|_{\infty}\lesssim\varepsilon_{*}(z), (4.8)

where ε∗\varepsilon_{*} is defined in (4.5).

Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 are direct consequences of Theorem 4.2: the former follows by the standard Stieltjes inversion argument, while the latter follows by the standard Green-function argument; see, for instance, [29, Section 18.5].

The remainder of this subsection presents the proof scheme for Theorem 4.2. We begin by propagating the local estimates from the large-|z||z| regime, where they follow directly from a Neumann expansion, to the whole spectral domain under consideration. For this purpose, we introduce two nested good events Ω−​(z)⊂Ω​(z)\Omega^{-}(z)\subset\Omega(z). The event Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) records the estimates that are stable under a small variation of the spectral parameter, whereas Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z) contains an additional margin in the error bounds. The main one-step improvement shows that, up to an arbitrarily small probability, membership in Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) can be upgraded to membership in Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z). Starting from large |z||z| and iterating this improvement along a sufficiently fine spectral lattice then yields the desired estimates uniformly in zz.

We first introduce the basic good event Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z).

Definition 4.3 (The set Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z)).

For z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}), we define the set of spectral regular graphs Ω⁡(z)⊂Ω¯\Omega(z)\subset\bar{\Omega} to be the set of graphs 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} such that

|Q−m|∞⩽ε∗​(z),|R⁡(Q⁡(𝒢,z),z)|∞+maxi,j∈𝔾⁡|Gi​j​(z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢),Q⁡(𝒢,z)),z)|⩽ε⁡(z).\displaystyle|Q-m|_{\infty}\leqslant\varepsilon_{*}(z),\quad|R(Q({\mathcal{G}},z),z)|_{\infty}+\max_{i,j\in{\mathbb{G}}}\left|G_{ij}(z)-G_{ij}\left(\mathrm{Ext}\bigl({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}),Q({\mathcal{G}},z)\bigr),z\right)\right|\leqslant\varepsilon(z). (4.9)

To carry out the iteration, we also define the event Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z), which imposes a stronger error bound.

Definition 4.4 (The set Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z)).

For z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}), we define Ω−​(z)⊂Ω⁡(z)⊂Ω¯\Omega^{-}(z)\subset\Omega(z)\subset\bar{\Omega} to be the set of graphs 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} such that

|Q−m|∞⩽ε∗​(z)2,|R⁡(Q⁡(𝒢,z),z)|∞+maxi,j∈𝔾⁡|Gi​j​(z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢),Q⁡(𝒢,z)),z)|⩽ε⁡(z)2.\displaystyle|Q-m|_{\infty}\leqslant\frac{\varepsilon_{*}(z)}{2},\quad|R(Q({\mathcal{G}},z),z)|_{\infty}+\max_{i,j\in{\mathbb{G}}}\left|G_{ij}(z)-G_{ij}\left(\mathrm{Ext}\bigl({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}),Q({\mathcal{G}},z)\bigr),z\right)\right|\leqslant\frac{\varepsilon(z)}{2}. (4.10)

Compared with Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z), the event Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z) improves the defining error bound from ε⁡(z)\varepsilon(z) to ε⁡(z)/2\varepsilon(z)/2. This margin is essential for the continuation argument: after moving the spectral parameter to a nearby point, Lipschitz continuity may consume part of the available error, but the graph still remains in Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z). The one-step improvement below can then be applied once again to recover membership in Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z).

The following proposition provides the starting point of the continuation argument. It shows that, when |z||z| is sufficiently large, every graph in Ω¯\bar{\Omega} already satisfies the stronger estimates defining Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z).

Proposition 4.5.

We have Ω¯⊂Ω−​(z)\bar{\Omega}\subset\Omega^{-}(z) uniformly for every z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with |z|⩾2​dmax|z|\geqslant 2d_{\rm max}. Here Ω¯\bar{\Omega} and Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z) are defined in Definition 1.1 and Definition 4.4 respectively.

Proof.

Fix 𝒢∈Ω¯{\mathcal{G}}\in\bar{\Omega} and |z|⩾2​dmax|z|\geqslant 2d_{\max}. Enlarging β\beta in Proposition 2.12 if necessary, we may assume that β⩾1/4\beta\geqslant 1/4. Since |z|⩾2​dmax|z|\geqslant 2d_{\max}, the Neumann expansions for 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} and its tree extensions converge absolutely. Any walk from ii to jj which distinguishes 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} from its radius-rr local extension must leave ℬr​({i,j},𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}) and return, and hence has length at least 2​r+22r+2. Consequently,

|Gi​j​(z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢),m⁡(z)),z)|⩽2​∑k⩾2​r+2dmaxk|z|k+1≲βr|z|3.\left|G_{ij}(z)-G_{ij}\left(\mathrm{Ext}\bigl({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}),m(z)\bigr),z\right)\right|\leqslant 2\sum_{k\geqslant 2r+2}\frac{d_{\max}^{k}}{|z|^{k+1}}\lesssim\frac{\beta^{r}}{|z|^{3}}. (4.11)

Recall that 1⩽r⩽ℜ1\leqslant r\leqslant{\mathfrak{R}}. If xx has a radius-ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} tree neighborhood, then we have Gx​x​(Ext⁡(ℬr​(x,𝒢),m),z)=mx​(z)G_{xx}\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(x,{\mathcal{G}}),m),z\bigr)=m_{x}(z) and Gx​xe​(Ext⁡(ℬr​(x,𝒢),m),z)=−mx​(z)​me​(z)G_{xx_{e}}\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(x,{\mathcal{G}}),m),z\bigr)=-m_{x}(z)m_{e}(z) where xex_{e} denotes the unique neighbor of xx such that the edge (x,xe)(x,x_{e}) is of type ee. Since (Ak)x​xe(A^{k})_{xx_{e}} counts the walks of length kk from xx to xex_{e}, and 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} agrees with its universal-cover extension inside ℬr​(x,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(x,{\mathcal{G}}), the two Neumann expansions agree for all k<2​r+1k<2r+1. Indeed, any walk from xx to xex_{e} that leaves ℬr​(x,𝒢){\mathcal{B}}_{r}(x,{\mathcal{G}}) has length at least (r+1)+r=2​r+1(r+1)+r=2r+1. Hence

|Gx​xe​(z)+mπ⁡(x)​(z)​me​(z)|⩽2​∑k⩾2​r+1dmaxk|z|k+1≲βr|z|3.\left|G_{xx_{e}}(z)+m_{\pi(x)}(z)m_{e}(z)\right|\leqslant 2\sum_{k\geqslant 2r+1}\frac{d_{\max}^{k}}{|z|^{k+1}}\lesssim\frac{\beta^{r}}{|z|^{3}}.

There are at most O⁡(N𝔠)\OO(N^{\mathfrak{c}}) exceptional vertices. For these vertices, the Neumann expansion, together with the vanishing diagonal and unit adjacency entries along edges, gives

Gx​x​(z)\displaystyle G_{xx}(z) =−1z+O⁡(|z|−3),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{z}+\OO(|z|^{-3}), mx​(z)\displaystyle m_{x}(z) =−1z+O⁡(|z|−3),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{z}+\OO(|z|^{-3}),
Gx​xe​(z)\displaystyle G_{xx_{e}}(z) =−1z2+O⁡(|z|−3),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{z^{2}}+\OO(|z|^{-3}), −mx​(z)​me​(z)\displaystyle-m_{x}(z)m_{e}(z) =−1z2+O⁡(|z|−4).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{z^{2}}+\OO(|z|^{-4}).

Averaging these estimates over each fiber, and using (4.11) for the nonexceptional diagonal entries, we obtain |Qver−mver|∞+maxe∈E→ℋ⁡|pe+mt⁡(e)​me|≲|z|−3​(βr+N−1+𝔠).|Q^{\rm ver}-m^{\rm ver}|_{\infty}+\max_{e\in\vec{E}_{\mathcal{H}}}\left|p_{e}+m_{t(e)}m_{e}\right|\lesssim|z|^{-3}(\beta^{r}+N^{-1+{\mathfrak{c}}}). The Neumann expansion also gives |Qt⁡(e)|,|me|∼|z|−1|Q_{t(e)}|,|m_{e}|\sim|z|^{-1} uniformly in this region. Using Qe=−pe/Qt⁡(e)Q_{e}=-p_{e}/Q_{t(e)} from (1.5), we have the exact identity Qe−me=−(pe+mt⁡(e)me)/Qt⁡(e)−me(Qt⁡(e)−mt⁡(e))/Qt⁡(e).Q_{e}-m_{e}=-(p_{e}+m_{t(e)}m_{e})/Q_{t(e)}-m_{e}\bigl(Q_{t(e)}-m_{t(e)}\bigr)/Q_{t(e)}. Therefore,

|Qver−mver|∞≲βr+N−1+𝔠|z|3≲βr|z|3,|Q−m|∞≲βr+N−1+𝔠|z|2≲βr|z|2≲βr,\displaystyle|Q^{\rm ver}-m^{\rm ver}|_{\infty}\lesssim\frac{\beta^{r}+N^{-1+{\mathfrak{c}}}}{|z|^{3}}\lesssim\frac{\beta^{r}}{|z|^{3}},\qquad|Q-m|_{\infty}\lesssim\frac{\beta^{r}+N^{-1+{\mathfrak{c}}}}{|z|^{2}}\lesssim\frac{\beta^{r}}{|z|^{2}}\lesssim\beta^{r}, (4.12)

where we used the parameter condition N−1+𝔠≲βrN^{-1+{\mathfrak{c}}}\lesssim\beta^{r}.

In particular, |Qe|,|me|∼|z|−1|Q_{e}|,|m_{e}|\sim|z|^{-1} for sufficiently large NN. The identity R⁡(Q,z)=(Q−m)/(Q​m)−B⁡(Q−m)R(Q,z)=(Q-m)/(Qm)-B(Q-m) therefore implies

|R⁡(Q,z)|∞≲(1+|z|2)​|Q−m|∞≲βr.|R(Q,z)|_{\infty}\lesssim(1+|z|^{2})|Q-m|_{\infty}\lesssim\beta^{r}. (4.13)

Finally, Lemma 2.20 implies that replacing mm by QQ changes the boundary self-energy by a matrix of operator norm O⁡(|Q−m|∞)\OO(|Q-m|_{\infty}). The exact tree-extension resolvent, restricted to the local core, has operator norm at most (|z|−dmax)−1(|z|-d_{\max})^{-1}. Thus a Neumann perturbation in the boundary weights yields

|Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢),Q),z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢),m),z)|≲|Q−m|∞|z|2≲βr.\left|G_{ij}\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}),Q),z\bigr)-G_{ij}\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}),m),z\bigr)\right|\lesssim\frac{|Q-m|_{\infty}}{|z|^{2}}\lesssim\beta^{r}.

Combining this with (4.11)–(4.13), we conclude that

|R⁡(Q,z)|∞+maxi,j∈𝔾⁡|Gi​j​(z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢),Q),z)|≲βr.|R(Q,z)|_{\infty}+\max_{i,j\in{\mathbb{G}}}\left|G_{ij}(z)-G_{ij}\left(\mathrm{Ext}\bigl({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}),Q\bigr),z\right)\right|\lesssim\beta^{r}.

By the parameter condition βr≪ε≲ε∗\beta^{r}\ll\varepsilon\lesssim\varepsilon_{*} uniformly in the region under consideration, the above inequality and (4.12) imply 𝒢∈Ω−​(z){\mathcal{G}}\in\Omega^{-}(z). ∎

The following proposition is the key one-step improvement. It states that, apart from an arbitrarily small exceptional probability, every graph satisfying the estimates of Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) in fact satisfies the stronger estimates of Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z) at the same spectral parameter. Consequently, once the weaker estimates have been propagated to a nearby value of zz by continuity, this proposition restores the extra margin needed for the next step of the iteration.

Proposition 4.6.

For any large 𝔮,N∈ℕ+{\mathfrak{q}},N\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, we have

ℙ⁡(Ω⁡(z)∖Ω−​(z))=O⁡(N−𝔮+1),\mathbb{P}(\Omega(z)\setminus\Omega^{-}(z))=\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}+1}), (4.14)

uniformly for every z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with |z|⩽2​dmax|z|\leqslant 2d_{\rm max} and η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{\mathfrak{b}}/N. Here Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) and Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z) are defined in Definition 4.3 and 4.4 respectively.

The main ingredients of the proof are the local resampling estimates, concentration of the boundary terms, and the resulting self-consistent equation. We defer the proof to Section 4.3.

The following proposition explains how the large-|z||z| initial estimate and the one-step improvement yield the local law uniformly throughout the spectral domain.

Proposition 4.7.

For any large 𝔮>0{\mathfrak{q}}>0 and NN sufficiently large, with probability 1−O⁡(N−𝔮)1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}) with respect to the uniform measure on Ω¯\bar{\Omega}, a graph 𝒢∈Ω¯{\mathcal{G}}\in\bar{\Omega} belongs to Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z) uniformly for all z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N.\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{{\mathfrak{b}}}/N.

Proof.

The proof follows exactly the same argument as [42, Proposition 4.9]; we therefore only indicate the main idea. By Proposition 4.5, we have Ω¯⊂Ω−​(z)\bar{\Omega}\subset\Omega^{-}(z) for |z|⩾2​dmax|z|\geqslant 2d_{\rm max}, which provides the starting point of the bootstrap. We then move from this region to {z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ):η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N}\{z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}):\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{\mathfrak{b}}/N\} along a sufficiently fine deterministic lattice in the spectral parameter with mesh size N−1N^{-1}. By the Lipschitz continuity of the resolvent and of Q⁡(𝒢,z)Q({\mathcal{G}},z) in zz, membership in Ω−\Omega^{-} at one lattice point implies membership in Ω\Omega at the next one, while Proposition 4.6 upgrades this to membership in Ω−\Omega^{-} with probability 1−O⁡(N−𝔮)1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}).

Iterating this argument over the lattice and using the same Lipschitz continuity to pass from the lattice to all spectral parameters gives

ℙ(𝒢∈Ω−(z) uniformly for all z∈ℂ+(ℐδ),η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟N)=1−O(N−𝔮).\mathbb{P}\left({\mathcal{G}}\in\Omega^{-}(z)\text{ uniformly for all }z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}),\ \eta\geqslant\frac{(\log N)^{\mathfrak{b}}}{N}\right)=1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}).

Here we apply Proposition 4.6 with a larger value of 𝔮{\mathfrak{q}} if necessary, so that the polynomial loss from the union bound over the spectral lattice is absorbed. ∎

We next turn to the proof of Theorem 4.2. The main difference between its conclusion and that of Proposition 4.7 is that the weights attached to the boundary in the local comparison graph are given by the deterministic Dyson solution mm, rather than by the empirical weights QQ.

Proof of Theorem 4.2.

Since we already have Proposition 4.7, it is sufficient to prove that, for every 𝒢∈Ω−​(z){\mathcal{G}}\in\Omega^{-}(z), its Green’s function satisfies (4.7) and (4.8). Since Lemma 2.20 implies that replacing QQ by mm gives an error O⁡(|Q−m|∞)\OO(|Q-m|_{\infty}), it follows from (4.10) that

|Gi​j​(z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢),m⁡(z)),z)|≲ε+ε∗≲ε∗,\left|G_{ij}(z)-G_{ij}\left(\mathrm{Ext}\bigl({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}),m(z)\bigr),z\right)\right|\lesssim\varepsilon+\varepsilon_{*}\lesssim\varepsilon_{*},

which proves (4.7). Averaging the above estimate over the diagonal entries in each fiber, and using that all but at most O⁡(N𝔠)\OO(N^{\mathfrak{c}}) vertices have a radius-ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} tree neighborhood, we obtain

|Qver​(z)−mver​(z)|∞≲ε∗+N−1+𝔠≲ε∗,|Q^{\rm ver}(z)-m^{\rm ver}(z)|_{\infty}\lesssim\varepsilon_{*}+N^{-1+{\mathfrak{c}}}\lesssim\varepsilon_{*},

which proves (4.8). ∎

It therefore remains only to prove Proposition 4.6. In the next subsection, we establish this result through two key propositions.

4.3 Two key propositions

We now turn to the proof of Proposition 4.6. The argument is based on two successive local resampling steps around a fixed root oo. Roughly speaking, the first resampling transfers the global estimates encoded in Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) to a local event Ωo+​(z)\Omega_{o}^{+}(z) that is stable under the filled switching construction. The second resampling produces the stronger rootwise event Ωo−​(z)\Omega_{o}^{-}(z), which contains the improved estimates needed to close the iteration.

Before defining the local event Ωo+​(z)\Omega_{o}^{+}(z), we introduce the filled exterior associated with 𝕋\mathbb{T}. Recall that 𝒢(𝕋){\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})} denotes the graph obtained from 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} by removing 𝕋\mathbb{T}. We define 𝒢⟨𝕋⟩:=TE⁡(𝒢(𝕋)),{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}:=\mathrm{TE}\bigl({\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}\bigr), where TE⁡(⋅)\mathrm{TE}(\cdot) is the tree-extension operator defined in Definition 2.14. The construction is illustrated in Figure 5. We denote the Green function of 𝒢⟨𝕋⟩{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle} by G⟨𝕋⟩​(z).G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}(z).

Definition 4.8 (The set Ωo+​(z)\Omega_{o}^{+}(z)).

For z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{{\mathfrak{b}}}/N, let 𝒯=ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z){\mathcal{T}}={\mathcal{B}}^{\rm ell}_{\ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z) with fixed root o∈𝔾o\in{\mathbb{G}}. We define Ωo+​(z)⊂Ω¯+\Omega_{o}^{+}(z)\subset\bar{\Omega}^{+} to be the set of graphs 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} such that

|Q−m|∞≲ε∗​(z),maxi,j∈𝔾∖𝕋⁡|Gi​j⟨𝕋⟩​(z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢⟨𝕋⟩),Q⁡(𝒢,z)),z)|≲(log⁡N)​ε​(z),\displaystyle|Q-m|_{\infty}\lesssim\varepsilon_{*}(z),\qquad\qquad\max_{i,j\in{\mathbb{G}}\setminus\mathbb{T}}\left|G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{ij}(z)-G_{ij}\left(\mathrm{Ext}\bigl({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}),Q({\mathcal{G}},z)\bigr),z\right)\right|\lesssim(\log N)\varepsilon(z), (4.15)
|R⁡(Q⁡(𝒢,z),z)|∞≲ε⁡(z),maxi,j∈𝔾⁡|Gi​j​(z)−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢),Q⁡(𝒢,z)),z)|≲(log⁡N)3​ε​(z).\displaystyle|R(Q({\mathcal{G}},z),z)|_{\infty}\lesssim\varepsilon(z),\qquad\max_{i,j\in{\mathbb{G}}}\left|G_{ij}(z)-G_{ij}\left(\mathrm{Ext}\bigl({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},{\mathcal{G}}),Q({\mathcal{G}},z)\bigr),z\right)\right|\lesssim(\log N)^{3}\varepsilon(z). (4.16)

The first key proposition shows that these additional local estimates are inherited from the global good event Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) after one elliptic switching, except for a set of switching data of arbitrarily small probability. In this sense, Ωo+​(z)\Omega_{o}^{+}(z) is the intermediate event produced by the first local resampling.

Proposition 4.9.

Let z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{\mathfrak{b}}/N. Then for any 𝒢∈Ω⁡(z){\mathcal{G}}\in\Omega(z) and large 𝔮,N∈ℕ+{\mathfrak{q}},N\in\mathbb{N}_{+}, there exists F2​(𝒢)⊂𝖲​(𝒢)F_{2}({\mathcal{G}})\subset{\sf S}({\mathcal{G}}), defined in Proposition 5.8, with ℙ𝒢​(F2​(𝒢))=1−O⁡(N−𝔮)\mathbb{P}_{{\mathcal{G}}}(F_{2}({\mathcal{G}}))=1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}) such that for every switching data 𝐒∈F2​(𝒢){\bf S}\in F_{2}({\mathcal{G}}), the switched graph 𝒢~=T𝐒​(𝒢)∈Ωo+​(z)\widetilde{{\mathcal{G}}}=T_{\bf S}({\mathcal{G}})\in\Omega_{o}^{+}(z). Here, the sets Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) and Ωo+​(z)\Omega_{o}^{+}(z) are defined in Definitions 4.3 and 4.8.

The proof of the above proposition is in Section 5.

The event Ωo+​(z)\Omega_{o}^{+}(z) is sufficient to control the switched filled resolvent, but it does not yet contain the improvement needed to close the iteration. We therefore introduce a second local event Ωo−​(z)\Omega_{o}^{-}(z). It strengthens the approximation at the fixed root oo by the averaging gain 2−ℓ2^{-\ell} and, when the root has a tree neighborhood, also records the three-term Green-function relation that will later yield the improved Dyson residual.

Definition 4.10 (The set Ωo−​(z)\Omega_{o}^{-}(z)).

For z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in\mathbb{C}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{{\mathfrak{b}}}/N, let 𝒯=ℬℓell​(o,𝒢,z){\mathcal{T}}={\mathcal{B}}^{\rm ell}_{\ell}(o,{\mathcal{G}};z) with fixed root o∈𝔾o\in{\mathbb{G}}. We define Ωo−​(z)\Omega_{o}^{-}(z) to be the set of graphs 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} such that,

|R⁡(Q⁡(𝒢,z),z)|∞≲ε⁡(z),|Q−m|∞≲ε∗​(z)\displaystyle|R(Q({\mathcal{G}},z),z)|_{\infty}\lesssim\varepsilon(z),\qquad|Q-m|_{\infty}\lesssim\varepsilon_{*}(z) (4.17)
maxi∈𝔾⁡|Go​i−Go​i​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({o,i},𝒢),Q⁡(z)),z)|≲(log⁡N)3​ε​(z)2ℓ+log⁡N|R⁡(Q⁡(𝒢,z),z)|∞.\displaystyle\max_{i\in{\mathbb{G}}}\left|G_{oi}-G_{oi}\left(\operatorname{Ext}\bigl(\mathcal{B}_{r}(\{o,i\},\mathcal{G}),Q(z)\bigr),z\right)\right|\lesssim\frac{(\log N)^{3}\varepsilon(z)}{2^{\ell}}+\log N\big|R(Q({\mathcal{G}},z),z)\big|_{\infty}. (4.18)

Moreover, if oo has a radius-ℜ{\mathfrak{R}} tree neighborhood in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}, then for every neighbor vv of oo

|Go​v2−Go​v−Go​o​Gv​v|≲(log⁡N)3​ε​(z)4ℓ\left|G_{ov}^{2}-G_{ov}-G_{oo}G_{vv}\right|\lesssim\frac{(\log N)^{3}\varepsilon(z)}{4^{\ell}} (4.19)

The second key proposition is the corresponding improvement step. Starting from a graph in Ωo+​(z)\Omega_{o}^{+}(z), a second local resampling produces a graph in Ωo−​(z)\Omega_{o}^{-}(z) with overwhelming conditional probability.

Proposition 4.11.

Let z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{\mathfrak{b}}/N. Let us summarize the relations among the good events introduced so far. By definition and Proposition 4.9,

The event Ω−​(z)\Omega^{-}(z) is the strengthened version of Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z), with the same type of global estimates but with an additional margin in the error bounds.

The event Ωo+​(z)\Omega_{o}^{+}(z) is the local event associated with the first resampling step. Compared with Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z), it allows logarithmic losses in the original Green-function estimates, while introducing the corresponding control for the filled exterior 𝒢⟨𝕋⟩{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}. The event Ωo−​(z)\Omega_{o}^{-}(z) is the local event produced after the second resampling step. Its estimates are concentrated at the root oo and contain the additional averaging gain coming from the elliptic boundary. It also records the local three-term relation that will be used to improve the Dyson residual.

Accordingly, the two local events are related to Ω⁡(z)\Omega(z) through the successive high-probability transitions

Ω⁡(z)→first local resamplingΩo+​(z)→second local resamplingΩo−​(z).\Omega(z)\;\xrightarrow{\text{first local resampling}}\;\Omega_{o}^{+}(z)\;\xrightarrow{\text{second local resampling}}\;\Omega_{o}^{-}(z).

The key mechanism in the proof of Proposition 4.6 is to obtain Ωo−​(z)\Omega_{o}^{-}(z) simultaneously for all roots oo and then use the deterministic implication

Ω⁡(z)​⋂o∈𝔾Ωo−​(z)⊂Ω−​(z).\Omega(z)\bigcap_{o\in{\mathbb{G}}}\Omega_{o}^{-}(z)\subset\Omega^{-}(z).

The former follows from the two resampling propositions and a union bound over the roots, while the latter converts the resulting rootwise estimates into the desired global improvement. We now carry out this argument.

5 Proof of Proposition 4.9: Stability under local resampling

The purpose of this section is to prove Proposition 4.9, namely the stability of the local law under the first local resampling around a fixed root oo. The proof is organized around three operations: we first remove the elliptic neighborhood 𝕋\mathbb{T} and replace it by its filled exterior, then perform the admissible switchings on the exterior graph, and finally glue 𝕋\mathbb{T} back. The main task is to show that the local Green-function approximation remains stable throughout these operations.

We first recall and summarize the graph notation used in this section. The graph 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} denotes the original lift, while 𝒢⟨𝕋⟩:=TE⁡(𝒢(𝕋)){\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}:=\mathrm{TE}\bigl({\mathcal{G}}^{(\mathbb{T})}\bigr) is the filled exterior obtained by removing 𝕋\mathbb{T} and applying the tree extension. Given switching data 𝐒\mathbf{S}, we denote by 𝒢~:=T𝐒​(𝒢)\widetilde{{\mathcal{G}}}:=T_{\mathbf{S}}({\mathcal{G}}) the switched graph, and by 𝒢~⟨𝕋⟩\widetilde{{\mathcal{G}}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle} the graph obtained by performing the corresponding switchings on the filled exterior 𝒢⟨𝕋⟩{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}. Their Green functions are denoted respectively by

G,G⟨𝕋⟩,G~,G~⟨𝕋⟩.G,\qquad G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle},\qquad\widetilde{G},\qquad\widetilde{G}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}.

Thus, throughout this section, a tilde indicates the switched graph, while the superscript ⟨𝕋⟩\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle indicates the filled exterior obtained after removing 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

Thus the graph transformations and the corresponding Green functions may be summarized schematically as

𝒢→filled removal of ​𝕋𝒢⟨𝕋⟩→local switching𝒢~⟨𝕋⟩→glue back ​𝕋𝒢~=T𝐒​(𝒢)G⟶G⟨𝕋⟩⟶G~⟨𝕋⟩⟶G~.\begin{array}[]{ccccccc}{\mathcal{G}}&\xrightarrow{\ \text{filled removal of }\mathbb{T}\ }&{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}&\xrightarrow{\ \text{local switching}\ }&\widetilde{{\mathcal{G}}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}&\xrightarrow{\ \text{glue back }\mathbb{T}\ }&\widetilde{{\mathcal{G}}}=T_{\mathbf{S}}({\mathcal{G}})\\[5.69054pt] G&\longrightarrow&G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}&\longrightarrow&\widetilde{G}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}&\longrightarrow&\widetilde{G}.\end{array}

5.1 Woodbury Formula under Switching

In this subsection, we introduce a Woodbury expansion adapted to the switching arguments used throughout the paper. The basic observation is that a switching changes the adjacency matrix only through a finite-rank perturbation supported on the switching vertices. By comparing the true Green function with a suitable local reference Green function, the effect of switching can then be expressed in terms of the pre-existing approximation error.

Throughout this subsection, by a switching we mean the following pair switching. For vertices u,vu,v, write

Δu​v:=eu​ev𝖳+ev​eu𝖳.\Delta_{uv}:=e_{u}e_{v}^{\mathsf{T}}+e_{v}e_{u}^{\mathsf{T}}. (5.1)

For each α∈[[μ]]\alpha\in[\![{\mu}]\!], consider two pairs (xα,yα)(x_{\alpha},y_{\alpha}) and (xα⋆,yα⋆),(x_{\alpha}^{\star},y_{\alpha}^{\star}), and replace them by (xα,yα⋆)(x_{\alpha},y_{\alpha}^{\star}) and (xα⋆,yα).(x_{\alpha}^{\star},y_{\alpha}). We encode the corresponding change by

ξα:=Δxα​yα+Δxα⋆​yα⋆−Δxα​yα⋆−Δxα⋆​yα,Ξ:=∑α=1μξα.\xi_{\alpha}:=\Delta_{x_{\alpha}y_{\alpha}}+\Delta_{x_{\alpha}^{\star}y_{\alpha}^{\star}}-\Delta_{x_{\alpha}y_{\alpha}^{\star}}-\Delta_{x_{\alpha}^{\star}y_{\alpha}},\qquad\Xi:=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{\mu}\xi_{\alpha}. (5.2)

If HH and H~\widetilde{H} denote the adjacency matrices before and after the switchings, respectively, then we directly have H~−H=−Ξ.\widetilde{H}-H=-\Xi. Introduce

U:=(ex1−ex1⋆,…,exμ−exμ⋆),V:=(ey1−ey1⋆,…,eyμ−eyμ⋆).U:=\bigl(e_{x_{1}}-e_{x_{1}^{\star}},\ldots,e_{x_{\mu}}-e_{x_{\mu}^{\star}}\bigr),\qquad V:=\bigl(e_{y_{1}}-e_{y_{1}^{\star}},\ldots,e_{y_{\mu}}-e_{y_{\mu}^{\star}}\bigr). (5.3)

Then a direct expansion gives Ξ=U​V𝖳+V​U𝖳=(VU)​(UV)𝖳,\Xi=UV^{\mathsf{T}}+VU^{\mathsf{T}}=\begin{pmatrix}V&U\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}U&V\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}},

5.1.1 Woodbury formula

We recall the standard Woodbury identity. Let AA be an invertible matrix and let X,YX,Y be rectangular matrices such that 𝕀+Y𝖳​A−1​X\mathbb{I}+Y^{\mathsf{T}}A^{-1}X is invertible. The Woodbury formula gives

(A+X​Y𝖳)−1=A−1−A−1​X​(𝕀+Y𝖳​A−1​X)−1​Y𝖳​A−1.(A+XY^{\mathsf{T}})^{-1}=A^{-1}-A^{-1}X\bigl(\mathbb{I}+Y^{\mathsf{T}}A^{-1}X\bigr)^{-1}Y^{\mathsf{T}}A^{-1}. (5.4)

Let G:=(H−z)−1G:=(H-z)^{-1} and G~=(H~−z)−1.\widetilde{G}=(\widetilde{H}-z)^{-1}. Applying (5.4) to H~−H=−(VU)​(UV)𝖳\widetilde{H}-H=-\begin{pmatrix}V&U\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}U&V\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}, we obtain

G~−G=G​FG​G,where ​FG:=(VU)​(𝕀−(UV)𝖳​G​(VU))−1​(UV)𝖳.\widetilde{G}-G=GF_{G}G,\qquad\mbox{where~}F_{G}:=\begin{pmatrix}V&U\end{pmatrix}\left(\mathbb{I}-\begin{pmatrix}U&V\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}G\begin{pmatrix}V&U\end{pmatrix}\right)^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}U&V\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}. (5.5)

FG=(G−1−G~−1)​G~​G−1=Ξ​G~​(G~−1+Ξ)=Ξ+Ξ​G~​Ξ.\displaystyle F_{G}=\bigl(G^{-1}-\widetilde{G}^{-1}\bigr)\widetilde{G}G^{-1}=\Xi\widetilde{G}\bigl(\widetilde{G}^{-1}+\Xi\bigr)=\Xi+\Xi\widetilde{G}\Xi. (5.6)

This form will be particularly convenient for exploiting the geometry of the switching vertices.

Lemma 5.1 (Boundary factorization).

The switching kernel FGF_{G} admits the factorization

(VU)​(U𝖳​G~​UI+U𝖳​G~​VI+V𝖳​G~​UV𝖳​G~​V)​(V𝖳U𝖳)\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}V&U\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}U^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{G}U&I+U^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{G}V\\ I+V^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{G}U&V^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{G}V\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}V^{\mathsf{T}}\\ U^{\mathsf{T}}\end{pmatrix}
=V⁡(U𝖳​G~​U)​V𝖳+V⁡(I+U𝖳​G~​V)​U𝖳+U⁡(I+V𝖳​G~​U)​V𝖳+U⁡(V𝖳​G~​V)​U𝖳\displaystyle=V(U^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{G}U)V^{\mathsf{T}}+V(I+U^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{G}V)U^{\mathsf{T}}+U(I+V^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{G}U)V^{\mathsf{T}}+U(V^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{G}V)U^{\mathsf{T}}

5.1.2 Expansion of the Green function

In some cases, rather than using (5.8) directly, we compare GG with a localized reference Green function. More precisely, let 𝒦⊂𝒢\mathcal{K}\subset\mathcal{G} be a subgraph containing all vertices involved in the switching under consideration, and let QQ be the boundary weight used in the corresponding extension. We define the localized Green function on 𝒦\mathcal{K} by

G⁡(Ext⁡(𝒦,Q),z).G\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}(\mathcal{K},Q),z\bigr).

Since 𝕂\mathbb{K} is in general a proper subset of 𝔾{\mathbb{G}}, the matrix G⁡(Ext⁡(𝒦,Q),z)G\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}(\mathcal{K},Q),z\bigr) and the original Green matrix GG naturally act on spaces of different dimensions. For the purpose of the Woodbury comparison below, we identify G⁡(Ext⁡(𝒦,Q),z)G\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}(\mathcal{K},Q),z\bigr) with its zero extension to 𝔾×𝔾{\mathbb{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}}; namely, throughout this section we write

Px​y:={Gx​y​(Ext⁡(𝒦,Q),z),x,y∈𝕂,0,otherwise.P_{xy}:=\begin{cases}G_{xy}\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}(\mathcal{K},Q),z\bigr),&x,y\in\mathbb{K},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Thus PP is regarded as a matrix on the same ambient vertex space 𝔾{\mathbb{G}}. This convention is only an embedding of the localized Green matrix into the ambient matrix space.

Let 𝒦~\widetilde{\mathcal{K}} be the graph obtained from 𝒦\mathcal{K} by performing the same pair switchings as in 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and define the localized Green function after switching by G⁡(Ext⁡(𝒦~,Q),z).G\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}(\widetilde{\mathcal{K}},Q),z\bigr). We again identify G⁡(Ext⁡(𝒦~,Q),z)G\bigl(\mathrm{Ext}(\widetilde{\mathcal{K}},Q),z\bigr) with its zero extension to 𝔾×𝔾{\mathbb{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}}, and denote it by P~\widetilde{P}. Since the switching vectors UU and VV are supported entirely in 𝕂\mathbb{K}, this zero-extension convention does not affect any of the Woodbury products appearing below.

Applying Lemma 5.1 on the localized vertex set 𝕂\mathbb{K}, and then extending the resulting identity by zero to 𝔾×𝔾{\mathbb{G}}\times{\mathbb{G}}, gives

P~−P=P​FP​P,where ​FP:=(VU)​(U𝖳​P~​UI+U𝖳​P~​VI+V𝖳​P~​UV𝖳​P~​V)​(VU)𝖳.\widetilde{P}-P=PF_{P}P,\qquad\mbox{where~}F_{P}:=\begin{pmatrix}V&U\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}U^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{P}U&I+U^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{P}V\\[2.84526pt] I+V^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{P}U&V^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{P}V\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}V&U\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}}. (5.9)

Then the graph geometry enters through the four compressed Green function matrices

U𝖳​P~​U,U𝖳​P~​V,V𝖳​P~​U,V𝖳​P~​V.U^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{P}U,\qquad U^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{P}V,\qquad V^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{P}U,\qquad V^{\mathsf{T}}\widetilde{P}V. (5.10)

For the different switching configurations considered in the rest of the paper, the geometry of the underlying graph often allows us to simplify the boundary kernel F∂F_{\partial} substantially. In particular, some of the above blocks may vanish identically, become diagonal or block diagonal, or admit sharper estimates due to separation and local tree structure. These further simplifications depend on the specific switching configuration and will therefore be carried out separately in the corresponding applications.

Set D:=G−P.D:=G-P. The quantity DD measures the error of the local approximation before switching. The following lemma gives an expansion of the difference G~−G\widetilde{G}-G in terms of the localized kernel matrix FPF_{P} and the local approximation error DD.

Assume that the corresponding Neumann series converges. Then

To control the Woodbury expansion, we need uniform summation bounds on the Green-function entries connecting the switching boundary. These estimates are used to bound both the effective boundary kernel F∂F_{\partial} and the transfer matrix WW appearing in Lemma 5.5. The following lemma provides the required bounds for the exterior and interior components.

5.3 Cell structure

The purpose of the cell structure is to isolate the possible interactions between different switching pairs. Although the sampled edges {bα,cα}\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\} are typically far apart, geometric separation alone is not sufficient for the subsequent Green function expansions, since two distant switching pairs may still interact through a relatively large off-diagonal Green function entry. We therefore group together precisely those switching supports which are either geometrically close or strongly coupled through the Green function. The main point is that such interactions are sparse with overwhelming probability, so that all but a small number of sampled pairs form isolated cells and may be treated essentially independently.

The sparsity of this cell structure is controlled by the Ward identity. Indeed, after obtaining a uniform bound on Im​Gx​x⟨𝕋⟩{\mathrm{Im}}G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{xx}, the Ward identity gives

∑y∈𝔾∖𝕋|Gx​y⟨𝕋⟩|2≲Im​Gx​x⟨𝕋⟩η,\sum_{y\in{\mathbb{G}}\setminus\mathbb{T}}\left|G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{xy}\right|^{2}\lesssim\frac{{\mathrm{Im}}G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{xx}}{\eta},

and hence only a small number of vertices yy can satisfy |Gx​y⟨𝕋⟩|⩾φ|G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{xy}|\geqslant\varphi. Combined with the approximate uniformity of the sampled vertices bα,cαb_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}, this shows that only few switching pairs can interact with any fixed vertex or with one another. We now formalize this observation through the following cell decomposition.

Fix a graph 𝒢∈𝖦N​(ℋ){\mathcal{G}}\in{\sf G}_{N}({\mathcal{H}}). For x,y∈𝔾∖𝕋x,y\in{\mathbb{G}}\setminus\mathbb{T}, write x≃yx\simeq y if

dist𝒢⟨𝕋⟩​(x,y)⩽ℜ4or|Gx​y⟨𝕋⟩​(z)|⩾φ⁡(z).\mathrm{dist}_{{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}}(x,y)\leqslant\frac{{\mathfrak{R}}}{4}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\bigl|G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{xy}(z)\bigr|\geqslant\varphi(z). (5.28)

For two sets 𝕏,𝕐⊂𝔾∖𝕋{\mathbb{X}},\mathbb{Y}\subset{\mathbb{G}}\setminus\mathbb{T}, write 𝕏≃𝕐{\mathbb{X}}\simeq\mathbb{Y} if x≃yx\simeq y for some x∈𝕏x\in{\mathbb{X}} and y∈𝕐y\in\mathbb{Y}.

Definition 5.7 (Cell structure).

Starting from

{a1,…,aμ},{bα,cα},α∈𝖶S,\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{\mu}\},\qquad\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\},\quad\alpha\in\mathsf{W}_{S},

repeatedly merge any two sets related by ≃\simeq. The resulting sets are called cells and are denoted by 𝕊0,𝕊1,…,𝕊κ\mathbb{S}_{0},\mathbb{S}_{1},\ldots,\mathbb{S}_{\kappa}, where {a1,…,aμ}⊂𝕊0\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{\mu}\}\subset\mathbb{S}_{0}. We denote the set of indices corresponding to singleton-pair cells by

𝖴:={α∈𝖶S:{bα,cα}=𝕊s​ for some ​s⩾1}.\mathsf{U}:=\left\{\alpha\in\mathsf{W}_{S}:\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\}=\mathbb{S}_{s}\text{ for some }s\geqslant 1\right\}.

This is the analogue of [42, Definition 5.13], without the ℬ1{\mathcal{B}}_{1}-enlargement. In particular, for distinct cells 𝕊s\mathbb{S}_{s} and 𝕊t\mathbb{S}_{t},

dist𝒢⟨𝕋⟩​(𝕊s,𝕊t)>ℜ4,maxx∈𝕊sy∈𝕊t⁡|Gx​y⟨𝕋⟩​(z)|<φ⁡(z).\mathrm{dist}_{{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}}(\mathbb{S}_{s},\mathbb{S}_{t})>\frac{{\mathfrak{R}}}{4},\qquad\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathbb{S}_{s}\\ y\in\mathbb{S}_{t}\end{subarray}}\bigl|G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{xy}(z)\bigr|<\varphi(z). (5.29)

To include the added vertices lα⋆l_{\alpha}^{\star}, recall that each lα⋆l_{\alpha}^{\star} is the root of a covering branch attached to aαa_{\alpha} before switching. The covering-branch identity and the boundedness of the Dyson weights imply

|Gx​lα⋆⟨𝕋⟩​(z)|≲|Gx​aα⟨𝕋⟩​(z)|,x∈𝔾∖𝕋.\bigl|G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{xl_{\alpha}^{\star}}(z)\bigr|\lesssim\bigl|G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{xa_{\alpha}}(z)\bigr|,\qquad x\in{\mathbb{G}}\setminus\mathbb{T}.

Hence, we obtain, whenever {bα,cα}=𝕊s\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\}=\mathbb{S}_{s} for some s⩾1s\geqslant 1,

maxx∈{bα,cα}y∈𝕎S′′∖{bα,cα}⁡|Gx​y⟨𝕋⟩​(z)|≲φ⁡(z),\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\}\\ y\in\mathbb{W}_{S}^{\prime\prime}\setminus\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\}\end{subarray}}\bigl|G^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{xy}(z)\bigr|\lesssim\varphi(z), (5.30)

where 𝕎S′′:=∪β∈𝖶S{aβ,bβ,cβ,lβ⋆}.\mathbb{W}_{S}^{\prime\prime}:=\cup_{\beta\in\mathsf{W}_{S}}\{a_{\beta},b_{\beta},c_{\beta},l_{\beta}^{\star}\}.

We next refine the good geometric event from Proposition 3.11 by incorporating the Green’s function bounds and the resulting sparsity of the cell structure.

Proposition 5.8.

Fix z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{\mathfrak{b}}/N and let 𝒢∈Ω⁡(z){\mathcal{G}}\in\Omega(z) or Ωo+​(z)\Omega^{+}_{o}(z). For every large 𝔮>0{\mathfrak{q}}>0, there exists an event F2​(𝒢)⊂F1​(𝒢)⊂𝖲⁡(𝒢)F_{2}({\mathcal{G}})\subset F_{1}({\mathcal{G}})\subset\mathsf{S}({\mathcal{G}}), where F1​(𝒢)F_{1}({\mathcal{G}}) is defined in Proposition 3.11, with probability ℙ𝒢​(F2​(𝒢))=1−O⁡(N−𝔮)\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{G}}(F_{2}({\mathcal{G}}))=1-\OO(N^{-{\mathfrak{q}}}) such that the following estimates hold:

Proof.

For every x∈𝔾∖𝕋x\in{\mathbb{G}}\setminus\mathbb{T}, set 𝕍x:={u∈𝔾∖𝕋:|Gx​u⟨𝕋⟩|⩾φ}{\mathbb{V}}_{x}:=\{u\in{\mathbb{G}}\setminus\mathbb{T}:|G_{xu}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}|\geqslant\varphi\}. ≲(dmax−1)ℜ/4N+|𝕍x|N≲4−2​ℓ.\displaystyle\lesssim\frac{(d_{\rm max}-1)^{{\mathfrak{R}}/4}}{N}+\frac{|{\mathbb{V}}_{x}|}{N}\lesssim 4^{-2\ell}.

5.4 Stability under switching of the filled exterior graph

We next study the effect of the admissible switchings on the filled exterior graph 𝒢⟨𝕋⟩{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}. The goal of this subsection is to show that the local Green-function approximation remains stable after these switchings, and to obtain a sharper off-diagonal bound for isolated switching cells.

Proposition 5.9 (Stability under switching of the filled exterior graph).

Fix z∈ℂ+​(ℐδ)z\in{\mathbb{C}}_{+}(\mathcal{I}_{\delta}) with η⩾(log⁡N)𝔟/N\eta\geqslant(\log N)^{\mathfrak{b}}/N and let 𝒢∈Ω⁡(z){\mathcal{G}}\in\Omega(z) or Ωo+​(z)\Omega^{+}_{o}(z).     provided that

    eitheri=cβfor someβ∈𝖶S∖{α}ori≄{bα,cα}​and​dist𝒢~⟨𝕋⟩⁡(i,aα)⩾ℜ/4.\mbox{either}\qquad i=c_{\beta}\quad\text{for some}\quad\beta\in\mathsf{W}_{S}\setminus\{\alpha\}\qquad\mbox{or}\qquad i\not\simeq\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\}~\mbox{and}~\operatorname{dist}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}}(i,a_{\alpha})\geqslant\mathfrak{R}/4.

Recall 𝖶S⊂⟦1,μ⟧\mathsf{W}_{S}\subset\llbracket 1,\mu\rrbracket denotes the admissible switching indices. For every α∈𝖶S\alpha\in\mathsf{W}_{S}, the graph 𝒢⟨𝕋⟩\mathcal{G}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle} contains the two edges (aα,lα⋆)(a_{\alpha},l_{\alpha}^{\star}) and (bα,cα).(b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}). The switching replaces them by

(aα,lα⋆),(bα,cα)⟶(aα,bα),(cα,lα⋆).(a_{\alpha},l_{\alpha}^{\star}),\quad(b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha})\longrightarrow(a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha}),\quad(c_{\alpha},l_{\alpha}^{\star}). (5.35)

For α∉𝖶S\alpha\notin\mathsf{W}_{S}, no switching is performed. Since all switchings in this step act only on the exterior graph, the interior component 𝒢in{\mathcal{G}}^{\rm in} does not enter this subsection. The exterior component after all switchings is 𝒢~⟨𝕋⟩\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}, and its Green matrix is G~⟨𝕋⟩\widetilde{G}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}. We next modify the localized comparison graph so that it contains the same switching operations as the original graph. To this end, define the set of original vertices involved in the admissible switchings by

𝕎S:={aα,bα,cα:α∈𝖶S},\mathbb{W}_{S}:=\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\mathsf{W}_{S}\}, (5.36)

5.5 Stability after gluing back 𝕋\mathbb{T}

We next glue the elliptic neighborhood 𝕋\mathbb{T} back into the switched filled exterior. 5.6 Changing from QQ to Q~\widetilde{Q}

In this subsection, we compare the self-consistent quantities before and after the switching. Recall that the switching replaces the two edges {lα,aα}\{l_{\alpha},a_{\alpha}\} and {bα,cα}\{b_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\} by {lα,cα}\{l_{\alpha},c_{\alpha}\} and {aα,bα},\{a_{\alpha},b_{\alpha}\}, and denote the resulting graph by 𝒢~\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}. Although the switching changes the resolvent locally, its effect becomes much smaller after averaging over each fiber. 5.7 Proof of Proposition 4.9

Proposition 5.9 implies (4.15). On the other hand, Proposition 5.11, together with Lemma 2.23, yields uniformly in i,j∈𝔾i,j\in{\mathbb{G}},

|G~i​j−Gi​j​(Ext⁡(ℬr​({i,j},𝒢~),Q),z)|≲(log⁡N)3​ε.\left|\widetilde{G}_{ij}-G_{ij}\left(\mathrm{Ext}\bigl({\mathcal{B}}_{r}(\{i,j\},\widetilde{{\mathcal{G}}}),Q\bigr),z\right)\right|\lesssim(\log N)^{3}\varepsilon.

6 Proof of Proposition 4.11: Improved Local Approximation

In this section, we prove Proposition 4.11. We first establish concentration for the diagonal errors produced by the individual filled switchings and identify their mean. We then insert these estimates into the gluing expansion for 𝕋\mathbb{T} to obtain the improved local approximation, and finally use the three-term identity on the comparison tree to derive the corresponding root estimate.

Appendix A Properties of the Green’s functions

Throughout this paper, we repeatedly use some (well-known) identities for Green’s functions, which we collect in this appendix.

A.1 Resolvent identity

The following well-known identity is referred to the resolvent identity: for two invertible matrices AA and BB of the same size, we have

A−1−B−1=A−1​(B−A)​B−1=B−1​(B−A)​A−1.A^{-1}-B^{-1}=A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}=B^{-1}(B-A)A^{-1}. (A.1)

A.2 Schur complement formula

Given an N×NN\times N matrix MM and an index set 𝕋⊂𝔾\mathbb{T}\subset{\mathbb{G}}, recall that we denote by M|𝕋M|_{\mathbb{T}} the 𝕋×𝕋\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{T}-matrix obtained by restricting MM to 𝕋\mathbb{T}, and that by M(𝕋)=M|𝕋cM^{(\mathbb{T})}=M|_{\mathbb{T}^{c}}, where 𝕋c=𝔾∖𝕋\mathbb{T}^{c}={\mathbb{G}}\setminus\mathbb{T}, we denote the matrix obtained by removing the rows and columns corresponding to indices in 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

Thus, for any 𝕋⊂𝔾\mathbb{T}\subset{\mathbb{G}}, any real symmetric matrix HH can be written (up to rearrangement of indices) in the block form

H=[AB′BD],H=\begin{bmatrix}A&B^{\prime}\\ B&D\end{bmatrix},

with A=H|𝕋A=H|_{\mathbb{T}} and D=H(𝕋)D=H^{(\mathbb{T})}. The Schur complement formula asserts that, for any z∈ℂ+z\in{\mathbb{C}}^{+},

G=(H−z)−1=[(A−z−B′​G(𝕋)​B)−1−(A−z−B′​G(𝕋)​B)−1​B′​G(𝕋)−G(𝕋)​B​(A−z−B′​G(𝕋)​B)−1G(𝕋)+G(𝕋)​B​(A−z−B′​G(𝕋)​B)−1​B′​G(𝕋)],G=(H-z)^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}(A-z-B^{\prime}G^{(\mathbb{T})}B)^{-1}&-(A-z-B^{\prime}G^{(\mathbb{T})}B)^{-1}B^{\prime}G^{(\mathbb{T})}\\ -G^{(\mathbb{T})}B(A-z-B^{\prime}G^{(\mathbb{T})}B)^{-1}&G^{(\mathbb{T})}+G^{(\mathbb{T})}B(A-z-B^{\prime}G^{(\mathbb{T})}B)^{-1}B^{\prime}G^{(\mathbb{T})}\end{bmatrix}, (A.2)

where G(𝕋)=(D−z)−1G^{(\mathbb{T})}=(D-z)^{-1}. Throughout the paper, we often use the following special cases of (A.2):

G|𝕋=(A−z−B′G(𝕋)B)−1,G|𝕋​𝕋c=−G|𝕋B′G(𝕋),\displaystyle\begin{split}G|_{\mathbb{T}}=(A-z-B^{\prime}G^{(\mathbb{T})}B)^{-1},\qquad G|_{\mathbb{T}\mathbb{T}^{c}}=-G|_{\mathbb{T}}B^{\prime}G^{(\mathbb{T})},\end{split} (A.3)

as well as the special case

Gi​j(k)=Gi​j−Gi​k​Gk​jGk​k.G_{ij}^{(k)}=G_{ij}-\frac{G_{ik}G_{kj}}{G_{kk}}. (A.4)

A.3 Ward identity

For any real symmetric N×NN\times N matrix AA, its Green’s function G⁡(z)=(A−z)−1G(z)=(A-z)^{-1} satisfies the Ward identity

∑j=1N|Gi​j​(z)|2=Im⁡Gi​i​(z)η,\sum_{j=1}^{N}|G_{ij}(z)|^{2}=\frac{\im G_{ii}(z)}{\eta}, (A.5)

where η=Im⁡[z]\eta={\mathrm{Im}}[z]. This identity provides a bound for the sum ∑j=1N|Gi​j​(z)|2\sum_{j=1}^{N}|G_{ij}(z)|^{2} in terms of the diagonal entries of the Green’s function.

A.4 Covering map

Lemma A.1 (Lemma B.1 in [15]).

Given a covering π:𝒢~→𝒢\pi:\tilde{\mathcal{G}}\to{\mathcal{G}} of graphs, denote the Green’s function of 𝒢~\tilde{\mathcal{G}} by G~\tilde{G} and that of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} by GG. Then for all vertices i,ji,j in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}, the Green’s functions obey

Gi​j=∑y:π⁡(y)=jG~x​y,\displaystyle G_{ij}=\sum_{y:\pi(y)=j}\tilde{G}_{xy}, (A.6)

where xx is any vertex of 𝒢~\tilde{\mathcal{G}} with π⁡(x)=i\pi(x)=i, provided the right hand side of (A.6) converges.

Therefore the lα⋆l_{\alpha}^{\star}-coordinate in (C.7) can be absorbed into the aαa_{\alpha}-coordinate. Indeed, in the product W​D⟨𝕋⟩WD^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}, the contributions from the lα⋆l_{\alpha}^{\star}- and aαa_{\alpha}-coordinates are

=\displaystyle={} −maα​lα(P~w​aα⟨𝕋⟩−P~w​cα⟨𝕋⟩)Daα⋅⟨𝕋⟩−(P~w​bα⟨𝕋⟩+maα​lαP~w​cα⟨𝕋⟩)Daα⋅⟨𝕋⟩=−(P~w​bα⟨𝕋⟩+maα​lαP~w​aα⟨𝕋⟩)Daα⋅⟨𝕋⟩,\displaystyle-m_{a_{\alpha}l_{\alpha}}\bigl(\widetilde{P}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{wa_{\alpha}}-\widetilde{P}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{wc_{\alpha}}\bigr)D^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{a_{\alpha}\,\cdot}-\bigl(\widetilde{P}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{wb_{\alpha}}+m_{a_{\alpha}l_{\alpha}}\widetilde{P}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{wc_{\alpha}}\bigr)D^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{a_{\alpha}\,\cdot}=-\bigl(\widetilde{P}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{wb_{\alpha}}+m_{a_{\alpha}l_{\alpha}}\widetilde{P}^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{wa_{\alpha}}\bigr)D^{\langle\mathbb{T}\rangle}_{a_{\alpha}\,\cdot},

where

where
